sections.title: A practical home for your next app

blocks.text: SoftN brings an editable interface, application logic and local data together in one portable app. Shape an app visually in Builder, describe it to your own AI provider in Studio, or write the source yourself. Runtime opens the result so you can use it.

These guides follow the decisions you actually make: what to build, which tool to open, which language to write logic in, where records live and how to share the app. You do not need to understand a virtual machine before changing a heading.

sections.title: Understand the pieces as you need them

blocks.text: A `.ui` file describes the interface. Logic, written in JavaScript (`.logic` files) or Python (`.py` files), runs in the ZIPP engine. XDB keeps app-scoped records. The host is the browser, desktop application or website that runs the app and decides which capabilities it may use.

A `.softn` bundle carries the editable client. A private backend is a separate deployment. Keeping that line clear makes exports easier to understand and keeps private server material out of downloads.

The guides explain the workflow and the concepts, with small examples. They are not an exhaustive reference for every component property: follow the source links at the end of each page for the underlying files, and check the host you deploy to before relying on an optional capability.

This edition was checked against the SoftN repository source on 25 September 2026 (SoftN 0.0.15, ZIPP v0.0.21). Pages changed since then show their own date, and the engine they describe is ZIPP v0.0.35, the engine SoftN ships.

seo.description: What is SoftN? An open-source app platform: portable .softn files, visual and AI-assisted tools, app logic in JavaScript or Python, and browser or desktop hosts.

sections.title: One app you can open, edit and run

blocks.text: SoftN is an open-source UI language, visual builder and runtime for editable apps on the web and desktop. Its portable `.softn` format packages the interface, client logic, data seeds and assets, so an app can be reopened and changed rather than treated as a finished black box.

That gives you several ways to start: explore an existing app, change a project in Builder, describe an idea in Studio with an AI provider you configure, or write the source yourself. These are different routes into the same editable app, not separate product formats.

Opens and runs bundles: a browser library at `/web/` and a desktop loader.
The ZIP-based app bundle you can export, share, reopen and customise.

blocks.text: You do not need an AI account to open the Fieldnotes example, start a project in Builder or edit source by hand. AI-assisted generation is one optional way in.

sections.title: From useful forms to interactive experiences

blocks.text: The built-in component library covers layouts, forms, data displays, charts and dashboards. Audio, animation and Three.js scenes extend it to games and richer interactive apps, and a Python app can train small machine-learning models with torch, all subject to what the host supports and grants.

A small planner is a good first app because it exercises input, logic, records and presentation without external services. A connected business dashboard adds another layer: authenticated backend actions, a server database and an access policy.

sections.title: Portable does not mean every host is identical

blocks.text: The bundle carries the editable client. It does not carry a running backend, external credentials, another person’s records or permission grants. A browser host and a desktop host can offer different capabilities.

blocks.title: Keep ownership practical
blocks.text: Keep an exported bundle or a source-controlled project you can restore. Browser storage is useful working storage, but it should not be your only copy of something important.

SoftN, ZIPP and XDB have different jobs. SoftN renders the app and connects its parts; ZIPP runs its logic, in JavaScript or Python; XDB keeps local records. FormLogic is an optional hosted integration, not a prerequisite for a standalone app.

Open Fieldnotes in Builder, change a heading, preview the result and export it. Reopen the export in Runtime. That short loop shows the central promise of the format: the thing you run remains something you can edit.

sections.title: A small app you can read end to end

blocks.text: A new Builder project has this shape: an interface in `ui/main.ui` that links its logic file with `<logic src>`, and a counter in that file. The path is relative to the `.ui` file.

blocks.code:
<logic src="../logic/main.logic" />

<App theme="dark">
  <Stack direction="vertical" gap="md" padding="lg">
    <Heading level={1}>My first SoftN app</Heading>
    <Text>Count: {count}</Text>
    <Button variant="primary" @click={increment}>Increment</Button>
  </Stack>
</App>
blocks.caption: ui/main.ui: the interface, linked to its logic file.
logic/main.logic: state and a function, in JavaScript.

blocks.text: `count` is state. The Text expression displays it. The Button’s `@click` calls `increment`, which changes the state, and SoftN redraws what depends on it.

The same app in Python links `../logic/main.py`. A function that changes a top-level name declares it `global`, and the button calls it through an arrow, because a handler bound by name is passed the click event and a Python function with no parameter for it would fail.

blocks.code:
count = 0


def increment():
    global count
    count = count + 1
blocks.caption: logic/main.py: the same counter in Python.

blocks.code: <Button variant="primary" @click={() => increment()}>Increment</Button>
blocks.caption: In a Python app, call a function with no parameters through an arrow.

blocks.text: Add a reset function that sets `count` to zero, then bind a second Button to it. It uses the same state and event pattern without persistence or networking.

blocks.caption: Add this to logic/main.logic.
Or this to logic/main.py.

blocks.code: <Button @click={() => reset()}>Reset</Button>
blocks.caption: Place this beside the Increment button, inside the Stack. The arrow form works in either language.

blocks.text: A variable here is live app state, not a durable record. Closing and reopening the app is a different test from redrawing it. Use XDB when you are ready to keep records.

seo.title: SoftN Builder | SoftN Docs
seo.description: SoftN Builder: the Design, Data, Preview and Code views, new projects in JavaScript or Python, the logic dock, handler suggestions, torch, permissions and export.

blocks.text: Builder is where you shape an app you can inspect and keep editing. It has four views: Design, a visual canvas with a properties panel; Data, for collections and their seed records; Preview, the running app; and Code, the source of the open file.
Start a project with New, reopen a bundle with Open (Ctrl+O), or open Fieldnotes from the homepage. A visual change is a change to editable source, not a step away from it.

Builder shows as many panels beside the canvas as the window has room for: all of them from 1660 pixels wide, Properties and one other from 1234, and one at a time below that. Under 900 pixels, on a phone or a small tablet, the canvas keeps the screen and Components, Properties, Hierarchy, Files and Logic open as sheets from a bar at the bottom: tap a component to add it, and move the selected element with Move up and Move down.

sections.title: Start a project in JavaScript or Python

blocks.text: The Create New App dialog asks for an App Name, a Description, a Theme (Light, Dark or System), a Starter Template (Blank, Landing or Dashboard) and a Logic Language.

items.description: The default. Logic in `.logic` files, in JavaScript.
Logic in `.py` modules. Adds the Machine learning (torch) option, which lets the app import torch; you can change it later in Export.

blocks.text: Either way the project has `ui/main.ui`, linked to its logic with `<logic src>`, a starter counter in the logic file and an empty `assets/` folder. An app uses one language for all its logic.

The Logic dock under the canvas edits the file the active page links with `<logic src>`, in that file’s language: a badge says JavaScript or Python, and the header shows the path. When the page links no logic, the dock shows the entry page’s. Hide it, and Show Logic Panel brings it back.

A page that still keeps its logic inline, in a `<logic>` block, is edited in Code view, and the dock offers Move logic to a file. That moves the block into a linked file and never overwrites a file that already holds other logic. A saved session whose entry page has inline logic is moved the same way when it is restored, when nothing would be lost.

In the properties panel, an event field such as a Button’s click suggests the functions the linked logic file defines, shown as `name(params)`. Choosing a Python function with no parameters inserts `() => name()`, because a handler bound by name is passed the event.
A handler can be any expression. A name the file does not define is kept, with a warning such as “No function named save in logic/main.py.”

A property field writes what it shows. In a text field, braces make an expression, `{user.name}`, and anything else is text. A field for an expression, such as a Modal’s `open` or a table’s `data`, takes the expression itself and writes it once it reads as a whole one. A checkbox, a number or a choice that a file binds to an expression is shown as that expression; empty it to get the usual control back. Emptying a field removes the property, so the component’s own default applies.

items: A path that already exists is refused: “… already exists. Choose another name.” This applies to creating, renaming and moving files and folders.
A `.py` file needs a Python module name: letters, digits and underscores. Reserved module names are refused, with the reason: `softn`, `torch`, `json`, `math` and anything starting `__softn`.
Two `.py` files with the same name in different folders are refused, because Python imports by module name.
Moving a file or renaming a folder rewrites every `<logic src>` that pointed at it.

Add a picture or file, in Files, puts a file of yours in the app, and Image and Avatar offer Add… beside their list of the app’s pictures. One file can be 50 MB at most. A picture can be replaced in place, keeping its name.
Renaming a picture or file rewrites every quoted path to it in the pages and the logic, `asset("…")` included, as one Undo step. Deleting one names the pages that use it first.
A logic file created without an extension gets the project’s: `.py` or `.logic`.

items.title: Edit the interface
items.text: In Design, select a component and change a property such as Text Content. Check the interaction in Preview, not only the canvas.

items.text: Use the Logic dock or Code view. Keep related changes small enough to test on their own.

items.title: Review the data

items.title: Preview and export
items.text: Check the sizes you support, export the bundle and reopen that exported copy.

blocks.text: Design writes a page’s template from the canvas and leaves the rest of the file exactly as it stands: the comment at its head, its `<logic>`, `<import>`, `<data>` and `<style>` blocks, and their order. Inside the template, a comment is kept with the element it stands before and shown above it on the canvas, and words with elements among them, such as a sentence with a key or a link in it, are shown as the words and elements they are.

A few constructs have no element to stay with: a comment directly before a closing tag, `#else` or `#empty`, or a comment inside braces. Code view marks each file Visual + source or Source-only; a Source-only file is edited as text, with the reason shown, which protects its source rather than simplifying it until the canvas accepts it.
Use Design where it offers a clear control, and Code for complex behaviour and structures that do not round-trip through the canvas. After either, run the same user flow again.
SmartStats, SmartCards and SmartList are drawn on the canvas as themselves when their rows are written on the page, as the Dashboard starter writes them.

The Preview view runs the app at Desktop (1440×900), Tablet (768×1024) or Mobile (390×844). It composes the app the way the runtime does, so a problem Run would refuse, such as an undeclared `import torch`, shows here first; for that one, Preview offers Enable torch.

Live preview, at the end of the row of file tabs in Design, runs the app beside the canvas and follows each change a moment after you make it. The app is not started again for a change to a page or its styles: what you typed into it, and where you were in it, stay. A change to its logic starts it again with its variables carried over.

Preview keeps working while a logic file is open: it runs the entry page and says so. Responsive behaviour still depends on the layout you wrote, so check forms, navigation, long text and tables at the narrowest size you support.

sections.title: Preview data and exported seeds are different jobs

blocks.text: Preview has its own test records, while the Data view holds the seeds the bundle carries. An app that looks populated in Preview may still need careful seeds for a first-time user.

blocks.title: Test a fresh start
blocks.text: Reopen the exported bundle in a clean context and check empty lists, first records and initial settings. That tells you more than repeatedly testing your populated workspace.

Export (Ctrl+Shift+E) opens Export Bundle. What the app may use writes `permission.json`: the capabilities, the allowed hosts for network access and storage policies per collection. For a Python app, a Python section writes `config.python.packages` to `manifest.json`. Then choose Export .softn, Open in runtime… or Publish….
For a first project, stop when one core flow is reliable: create a record, show it, change it and reopen the export. Add polish after that path works.

sections.title: Turn a brief into an editable starting point

blocks.text: Studio is SoftN’s AI-assisted way to create an app. You connect a provider, describe the app, approve a plan, and an AI agent builds it: it reads and edits the files, checks the app after every change and fixes what breaks, until the app does what you asked. The result is ordinary SoftN source you can keep editing.

items.description: A model running on your computer through Ollama, LM Studio or another OpenAI-compatible server. Free and private; the server needs to allow requests from the page (CORS).
Your OpenAI account; OpenAI bills it for what the AI does.
Your Anthropic account; Anthropic bills it for what the AI does.
Any service that accepts the OpenAI chat-completions format, with its address and key.

blocks.text: On a first visit Studio asks you to connect one before anything else. After connecting it lists the provider’s own models for you to choose from, and Test connection explains a failure in plain words (a wrong key, a local server without CORS). The key is kept in this browser’s local storage, not encrypted, and sent only to the provider, straight from the browser. Settings lists your providers and opens the same setup to add or edit one.

AI generation is not required. From the dashboard you can Start a new app, Import a bundle (`.softn`, `.zip` or `.json`) or Start from an example, which needs no key: Reading list, in JavaScript, and Reading list in Python.

The brief has three parts, Basics, Structure and Style, and ends with Generate: in a window 1100 pixels wide or more they are one page, side by side, and in a narrower one they are three steps. Structure is where you choose the Logic language: JavaScript (`main.js`), the default, or Python (`main.py`). The whole app uses one language. With Python selected, Uses machine learning `torch` adds torch to `manifest.json`.

A useful description names the people using the app, the records they manage, the screens they need and what each important button does. Say what stays local and which operations, if any, need a backend.

blocks.code:
Create a local task planner for one person.

Screens: task list and a small summary dashboard.
Each task needs a title and completion status.
Let me add a task, mark it complete and filter the list.
Use local records. Do not add login, AI calls or a backend.
Make empty states clear and keep the phone layout readable.
blocks.caption: An example description. It is plain language, not a special command syntax.

blocks.text: Before any code is written, the Blueprint review shows the planned pages, data model, risks and assumptions. Approve blueprint, add a note and revise the plan, or go back with Revise brief. A line that adds or removes pages, such as “add a page for watering” or “remove the settings page”, changes the plan at once; any other line is kept as a note and sent to the AI at the start of every run. One complete loop is easier to review than many unfinished screens.

sections.title: How the AI builds your app

blocks.text: Approve and build on the blueprint, or any message in the chat, starts a run. The AI works in steps with tools: it lists, reads and searches files, writes a file or makes an exact edit inside one, looks up components and the SoftN guides, checks the app, inspects what the preview shows, and calls the app’s own functions to test that they work. It keeps a short plan you can watch, asks you a question when the brief leaves something open, and finishes with a summary.

After every step that changes files, Studio checks the app the way Run does — the composer, the validator and a real render — and hands any error back, so a mistake is fixed in the next step rather than left for you. A run cannot finish while the check fails.

items: The chat shows the run as a timeline: the plan, each step as a row you can open to see its diff or check report, and the AI’s notes between steps. The preview updates as files change.
Stop ends a run at any point; Continue picks it up again. A network failure pauses the run with Resume rather than losing it.
Every step that writes can be undone on its own, and Revert run undoes the whole run.

A run ends at its step limit or token budget, or after the same failure three times, and says which. Both limits, the automatic check and whether deleting files asks you first are in Settings, under Agent runs.
The AI only reads what it needs, so a large project does not make every request larger. It cannot change a file it has not read in the run, and it cannot write outside the project.

blocks.title: Ask for the result
blocks.text: Describe the result, not the steps: who uses the app, what they record, what each screen and button does. The AI plans the steps and checks its own work, and you can answer its questions as it goes.

The preview composes the app exactly as Run does. When the composer refuses the app, the canvas says “This app cannot be previewed as it stands.” with the reason, naming the file, and a View source expander. An undeclared `import torch` offers Enable torch, which adds torch to `config.python.packages`; Undo takes it back out.

The validator runs the same composer whenever the files or the blueprint change. While it reports a refusal, Run and Publish are disabled (“Fix what the validator found first”); Export bundle stays available, so you can take the files elsewhere to fix them. It also rejects a `.py` file under `server/`: server logic runs as JavaScript on every backend host.

The preview follows the files as they are written, by the AI or by you, without starting the app again: words and styles change with what the app held kept, and a new page appears in its navigation. A change to the logic starts it again with its variables carried over. A file that does not work yet leaves the last version that worked on screen, with a line saying what is wrong with the newest.

sections.title: Review the app, not only the generated text

items.title: Read the source and permissions
items.text: Check that the result matches the brief and does not ask for capabilities the app does not need.

items.title: Exercise the main interaction
items.text: Create, change and display a record. Try invalid input and the empty state.

items.title: Try narrow layouts
items.text: Check labels, controls and navigation at phone size.

items.title: Export and reopen
items.text: Check that the project survives the same bundle handoff as a hand-written app.

blocks.text: A new project is written as HTML pages: `index.html`, the page the app opens on, which names its code with `<script src="main.js">` and places each page of the blueprint from `pages/`, such as `pages/dashboard.html`; and `main.js`, or `main.py` in a Python app. Beside them are `manifest.json`, `permission.json`, an `xdb/` seed file for each collection, `assets/icon.svg`, and Studio’s own notes on the brief and blueprint under `builder/`. A project made before, with `.ui` pages under `ui/` and `.logic` files under `logic/`, still opens and is edited as it is.

Import takes a whole bundle. Logic files come in as text, `.py` included, and Export bundle lists the logic under `files.logic` in the manifest: `.logic` and `.py` files, and a `.js` file a page links or other logic imports, such as `main.js`. Server logic is left out of that group. The export is the same `.softn` format Builder and Runtime open.

An external AI provider can involve its own credentials, limits and charges. Review the configuration and the provider’s terms before sending content. Never put a private access token in app source or a downloadable bundle.

blocks.title: Generation is not validation
blocks.text: Generated logic and UI still need review. A convincing explanation is not proof that a function exists, an export is complete or a permission is granted.

Files is a file manager you can use without the AI. Right-click a file or folder, or use the “more” button on its row or the menu key, for New file, New folder, Add files, Rename (F2), Duplicate, Copy, Cut, Paste, Download, Copy path and Delete; drag a file onto a folder to move it. Add files with the button, by dropping them on the panel or by pasting: a copied picture arrives as `pasted-picture.png`.

items: Nothing is overwritten: a second `logo.png` becomes `logo-2.png`.
One file can be 50 MB at most; an app, 200 MB and 10,000 files.
Renaming or moving a file rewrites what refers to it in the same step, the manifest’s main page included. `manifest.json` and `permission.json` keep their names and places.
Each action is one named step in History, and Undo takes it back. Opening or importing a project is not a step, so Undo straight after it removes nothing.
While the AI is working, the panel does not write: its actions wait for the run to end or be stopped.

blocks.text: Refine the result in Studio or open the export in Builder. The useful outcome is an app whose behaviour you understand and whose source you can change, not a prompt you can never reproduce.

Open in Builder, on the project bar (the project menu on a phone), saves the project and opens it in the visual Builder in the same tab, under “From Studio” and the project’s name. Back to Studio brings the files you changed into the same project as one History step; a file changed on both sides is asked about. It is offered where Studio and Builder are served from one site, and not inside FormLogic.
For a connected app, describe the client and backend responsibilities separately. A generated interface is not, by itself, a deployed authentication system or private API.

pages.title: SoftN Runtime
pages.summary: Open bundles, switch between running apps and understand what the browser library does and does not keep.

seo.title: SoftN Runtime | SoftN Docs
seo.description: SoftN Runtime: open .softn bundles, browse apps, use the saved browser library, switch running apps, and see how it picks the engine for JavaScript or Python logic.

sections.title: The place to use an app

blocks.text: Runtime opens and runs `.softn` bundles. On the web, at `/web/`, it opens a bundle from the + button or a file dropped on the page, runs apps from the directory and keeps a library of what you opened in this browser. The desktop loader is a Tauri app (`npm run dev:desktop` in a checkout).
Creation tools change an app; Runtime uses it. The same bundle can be reopened in Builder or Studio when you want to customise it.

Runtime reads the app before it starts. Logic files ending `.py` make it a Python app, anything else a JavaScript one, and both run in the same engine: ZIPP’s javascript-python-base module, one WebAssembly file for both languages. A bundle the composer refuses, for example one that mixes the two languages or imports torch without declaring it, does not start, and the message says what to change.

sections.title: Home is not the same as Close

blocks.text: The web workspace keeps apps running when you return to its home view, so you can browse or open another app without losing an unfinished form. Use Home to switch between apps and Close to stop the current one.
Test this in your own app. Navigating within a running workspace, closing an app and reopening a saved bundle can involve different state and persistence.

sections.title: Edit an app while it runs

blocks.text: Edit, on the bar over a running app (in the ⋯ menu on a phone), opens its source beside it. What you change shows in the app after a short pause, with no refresh; a change to its logic starts it again with its variables carried over. A change that does not work yet is not shown: the last version that worked keeps running, and the editor says what is wrong and where.

Pick, then press an element, to see the lines that drew it and change its words and plain attributes in a small form. Handlers, bindings, conditions and anything the app works out are listed and left to the source. Undo, Redo and Restart are beside it, and the editor’s menu has Download the edited app, Publish it, Add a file and Discard my changes.

items: An app from the directory or a link is never changed: your first change makes your own copy in your library, named “(my copy)”, and that is what you edit and run from then on.

An app you opened from a file, or made in Studio or Builder, is edited as itself. Your changes are kept with it in this browser and are there after a reload; Discard my changes returns it to how it was opened.
A change to what an app asks permission for opens it again, and it asks you.
The app cannot open the editor, read it or tell that it is open, and there is no Edit where the runtime is embedded in another page.

blocks.text: Apps you open are kept in this browser’s library, with offline readiness shown for saved apps. That is not an account-wide backup: another device, another browser profile or cleared site storage can have different contents.

blocks.title: Check offline readiness before relying on it
blocks.text: A saved app may still use network services or remote resources. Test the real workflow without a connection, and keep a separate copy of important exports.

sections.title: The host decides what the app can reach

blocks.text: A capability needs support and permission from the host. The browser can also ask for its own consent for camera or microphone access. A desktop build may offer native storage or integrations an ordinary browser cannot.

Allow takes effect in the running app: it is not started again, and what you had typed stays. A call the app made while the question was up is kept, with nothing of it done, and made once you allow; Not now refuses it at once. The bar says beforehand in the few cases where allowing does start the app again, with its variables carried over.
The manifest name is not a storage account. The general bundle loader, single-app deployments and FormLogic each have identity rules that decide which records and grants an app sees.

items: Open the exported bundle, not only the editor preview.
Exercise the main flow, and return Home without losing unfinished input.
Close and reopen, then check which state is meant to persist.
Review permission requests, and test denial as well as approval.
Confirm the host and browser you actually plan to support.

blocks.text: When something differs between preview and Runtime, first work out whether the difference is UI state, data seeds, persistent records, host capability support or deployment configuration.

pages.title: The .softn app format
pages.summary: What a bundle contains, how its manifest configures logic and packages, what an export leaves behind, and how to think about seeds and permissions.

seo.title: The .softn app format | SoftN Docs
seo.description: The .softn format: a ZIP bundle with manifest.json, permission.json, UI, JavaScript or Python logic, XDB seeds and assets; config.execution and config.python.packages.

blocks.text: A `.softn` file is a ZIP-based app bundle holding the editable client material SoftN needs to load an app. It is the handoff between creation tools and runtimes: export an app, reopen it and change its source.
It does not contain every external dependency. A remote service, an AI provider or a private server database keeps its own deployment and access requirements.

blocks.code:
my-app.softn
├── manifest.json
├── permission.json
├── index.html
├── pages/
├── main.js
├── xdb/
└── assets/
blocks.caption: The layout Studio writes for a new project; a Python app has `main.py` in place of `main.js`. Builder’s new projects, and bundles made before, keep their pages in `ui/` and their logic in `logic/`. Exact files depend on the app.

items.description: App metadata, the entry file and optional configuration.
The capabilities the app requests from its host. Declaring one is not the same as being granted it.
The interface: pages written as HTML, with SoftN’s components and syntax in them. `.ui` files under `ui/`, as Builder writes them, are the same language; both open.
Client logic: JavaScript in `.js` files (`.logic` files under `logic/` in Builder’s projects), or Python in `.py` files such as `main.py`. One language per app.
Optional collection seeds carried with the app.
Images, styles, sounds, models and other distributable files.

blocks.text: `manifest.json` needs a `name` and a `main` entry, the path of the interface file that opens first; the rest is optional for opening an app. A `files` section listing the `ui`, `logic`, `xdb` and `assets` entries is conventional and is what the editors write, but a bundle without it still opens. The app directory’s publication check also asks for a `version` and warns when there is no `description`. `permission.json` is optional too: without it the app asks for nothing.

blocks.caption: A Python app that uses torch. Both config keys are optional.

items.description: `"main"`, the default, runs logic on the page’s thread; `"worker"` asks for a JavaScript app’s logic to run in a worker. Python logic always runs on the main thread. Any other value is reported and treated as main.

`"light"` or `"dark"` draws the app on that side in the web runtime, on a single-app page, in the desktop runtime and embedded in FormLogic, whatever the host’s own theme or the visitor’s device prefers. `"system"`, or no mode, follows the host instead. A page whose own `<App theme>` is light or dark keeps that side over this one. Builder writes the key from the project’s Theme setting; any other value is treated as system.
The Python packages the app imports. `torch` is the only one offered; any other name is refused. An `import torch` the manifest does not declare is refused too, with the line to add.

The sync server the app’s records are replicated through: a softn-server host (`apps/softn-host-rust/PRIVATE_BACKEND.md`). An `https` or `wss` address, with `/sync` added to its path unless it ends there; an `http` or `ws` address works only for this computer (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`). SoftN Web and the desktop runtime connect to it; a single-app page does not. It connects only when `permission.json` declares `sync` and the person allows it, and when `net` lists allowed_hosts, the server’s host must be one of them.

The sync token the host gives the app’s browsers. Everyone with the bundle can read it, and on the host it opens sync and nothing else. The host’s operator token is never sent for sync, `auth_token` included: keep it out of the bundle and give it to the host as `SOFTN_AUTH_TOKEN`.
The collections server sync carries, as a list of names. Without it, every collection the app has or starts to use.
Lists the logic files: JavaScript (`.js` or `.logic`) or Python (`.py`), never both. The file name alone decides the language.

items: A logic file whose name ends `.py` is Python; any other is JavaScript. Nothing else declares the language.
A bundle that mixes Python and JavaScript logic is refused: one engine reads both languages, but an app’s logic is read as one of them, so the two could not share names.
Python must live in a file referenced with `<script src>` or `<logic src>`. An inline `<logic lang="python">` block is refused, because reindenting markup could change the program.
Each `.py` file is a module named after the file, so two with the same name are refused, and the names `softn`, `torch`, `json`, `math` and anything starting `__softn` are reserved.
Server logic for the PHP and Rust hosts is JavaScript. Python is client logic only.

sections.title: Seeds are not a backup of live records

blocks.text: Seed records are starting content for a new app instance. The records someone creates while using the app belong to that host’s storage and identity rules. Exporting a project does not export every user’s live database.

Builder’s preview uses test records. Review the seeds you mean to distribute in the Data view, then test a fresh runtime instance, so a demo does not look complete only because it is using your local data.

sections.title: Separate client downloads from private deployment

blocks.text: Server hosts can run server-side `.logic` resources. The browser never executes those, and a backend deployment decides how to keep private scripts, credentials and SQLite databases on the server.

blocks.title: Assume a recipient can inspect the bundle
blocks.text: Anything in a downloadable client archive should be something you intend to share. An editable client bundle cannot hide a service secret or a private database.

sections.title: Identity and compatibility belong to the host too

blocks.text: The general bundle loader isolates bundles by digest. Single-app and FormLogic hosts provide their own deployment identity. An app name alone does not grant access to another app’s records or permission grants.
Test a bundle on the host you intend to use. A successful export confirms packaging, not browser microphone consent, backend authorisation or support for every optional capability.

pages.title: The SoftN UI language
pages.summary: Read component tags, expressions, bindings, event handlers and their modifiers, class and style directives, conditionals and loops, link a page to its logic file, and place one page inside another.

seo.title: The SoftN UI language | SoftN Docs
seo.description: SoftN .ui syntax: components, expression props, what an expression may contain, event handlers and modifiers, two-way binding, class: and style: directives, conditionals, loops, and one page placed inside another.

blocks.text: A `.ui` file describes the interface with component tags, properties and expressions. SoftN parses the source and renders it through React, but the app source is SoftN syntax: you do not rewrite it as JSX.

A page links its logic with `<logic src="../logic/main.logic" />`, a path relative to the `.ui` file; a Python app links a `.py` file the same way. JavaScript can also sit inline in a `<logic>` block; Python cannot.

sections.title: Write it as an HTML page

blocks.text: A page can be written the way an HTML page is written, and mix in SoftN’s components and syntax wherever it likes. Lower-case tags are HTML elements, `<div>`, `<span>`, `<a>`, `<table>`, `<form>` and the rest; capitalised tags are SoftN components, `<Button>`, `<Stack>`, `<DataGrid>`. The file can be called `index.html` and its code `main.js`: a page and its logic are found by what names them, `manifest.json`’s `main`, an `<import from>` or a `<script src>`, not by their file names, so `.ui` and `.logic` keep working beside them. Studio makes a new project this way (`index.html`, `pages/*.html`, `main.js`); the Builder’s own new projects are still `.ui` and `.logic`, and it opens and saves either. An app written this way runs in the browser runtime, in a standalone deployment and as a page of your own site.

blocks.title: Where a page is not HTML
blocks.text: Braces in text are expressions: write `\{` or `{"{"}` for a brace to show. A line that begins `#if`, `#each`, `#else` or `#end` is SoftN’s. A capitalised tag is a component’s, never HTML’s: `<Button>`, `<Input>` and `<Table>` are SoftN’s, so `<Input>` is not void, while `<button>` and `<BUTTON>` are HTML’s. A tag that ends `/>` ends there, `<div/>` too, where HTML would pass over the slash. A form inside a form is kept, a form written straight in a table holds its rows (so its fields are in it), and `</form>` closes what is still open inside the form; HTML would drop the inner form, leave the table’s form empty and leave the rest open. A `<b>` left open in a paragraph is opened again around the words of the next, but not around the space between tags: HTML would wrap every later paragraph in it. SoftN’s own syntax is read in any case, as HTML is: `#IF`, `#Else If`, `#EACH (item IN items)`, `#End`, `<IMPORT>`, `<LOGIC>`, `@CLICK`, `.PREVENT` and `:BIND`; and a component may be named in any case where no HTML element has its name, `<datagrid>` for `DataGrid`. And code and stylesheets from other sites are not loaded: an app’s code runs in its own sandbox, so the page’s code comes from the app’s own files. A `.js` file is SoftN logic: its top-level variables are the page’s state and its functions what the page calls, so `export` before a declaration is read as the declaration, and `import { total } from "./cart.js"` places that file’s code, whose names every file sees. An import that renames, a default or namespace import and a package import are not read. The page shows the state, and a handler changes the state; code that names `document` is also given one, the page’s own HTML to query and change, as the next section describes.

A page’s code can work on the page the way code in a browser does. Code that names `document` is given one: the page’s own HTML, there from the code’s first line, so an element written above the script is found by `document.getElementById` as it is in a browser. What the code changes is drawn, and what the person does to the page (a click, a key, what they type) reaches the code’s listeners. The code runs in SoftN’s sandbox as all logic does, and what it writes is drawn through the same checks as markup: `innerHTML` cannot bring in a `<script>`, an `<iframe>`, an `onerror` or a `javascript:` address.

items: `document`: `getElementById`, `querySelector` and `querySelectorAll` (tags, ids, classes, attributes, `>`, `+`, `~`, `:not()`, `:nth-child()`, `:first-child`, `:checked` and more), `createElement`, `createTextNode`, `createDocumentFragment`, `body`, `title`, `readyState`, and `DOMContentLoaded` once the page is drawn; `window.addEventListener("load", …)` runs then too.

Elements: `appendChild`, `append`, `prepend`, `insertBefore`, `remove`, `replaceWith`, `before`, `after`, `cloneNode`, `textContent`, `innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, `insertAdjacentHTML`, `getAttribute` and `setAttribute`, `classList`, `style` (`el.style.color = "red"`), `dataset`, `children`, `parentElement`, `closest`, `matches`, `focus()` and `click()`; boolean attributes as properties (`el.hidden = true`, `button.disabled`, `details.open`); `a.href` and `img.src` as whole addresses. A `<template>`’s `content` is copied with `cloneNode(true)`, and a `<dialog>` opens with `show()` or `showModal()` (drawn over the app, inside its box) and closes with `close()`, its form (`method="dialog"`) or Escape.

Events: `addEventListener` and `removeEventListener` with capture, bubbling and `once`, `preventDefault`, `stopPropagation`, `event.target`, `key`, `clientX` and the rest, `el.onclick = …`, and `onclick="…"` run as a browser runs it, with `this` and `event`: in HTML the code writes, and in the page’s own markup where it is code SoftN does not read (`onclick="this.classList.toggle('on')"`), on a page with code of its own or none.

Forms: a field’s `value` and `checked` are what the person typed or ticked; setting them changes the field; `new FormData(form)` reads a form, every choice of a `<select multiple>` included, and can be listed (`Object.fromEntries(new FormData(form))`); `form.elements.email` and `form.email` find a field by its name. A form checks itself as a browser does: `checkValidity()`, `reportValidity()`, `validity`, `validationMessage` and `setCustomValidity()` from `required`, `type`, `pattern`, `minlength`, `maxlength`, `min`, `max` and `step`, and `requestSubmit()` sends it only when it is valid. A `<form>` with no `action` stays on the page.

What SoftN draws (a component, a `{value}`, `#if` and `#each`) the code can find, move and remove, but not change inside. An event inside one reaches the code with its real target, read as the page shows it: `list.addEventListener("click", (e) => e.target.closest("li").dataset.id)` works on a list drawn with `#each`.

Also given: `fetch` (a promise; an address of the app’s own, `fetch("data.json")`, is read from its files with no network, and any other host only as `permission.json` allows `net`, with no cookie of the page), `location` (`location.href = "about.html"` goes to another page of the app, never to another site), `history` (`pushState`, `back()`, and `popstate` and `hashchange`, within the page), `URL`, `URLSearchParams`, `btoa` and `atob`, `TextEncoder` and `TextDecoder`, `crypto.randomUUID()` and `crypto.getRandomValues()` (random numbers to rely on), `structuredClone`, `AbortController`, `EventTarget`, `MutationObserver`, `matchMedia()`, `innerWidth`, `queueMicrotask`, `requestAnimationFrame`, `sessionStorage` and `alert()`, which is shown in the app; `confirm()` and `prompt()` cannot wait for an answer here, so ask with a `<Confirm>` or a field on the page. `document.title` names the browser tab where the app has the window to itself, and what the code puts on `document.body` and `document.documentElement` (a class, a style, a data attribute) is on the app’s root.

Layout is known once it has been asked for: the first `offsetWidth` or `getBoundingClientRect()` of an element is zero, and the host measures it then and whenever it changes size, which a `ResizeObserver` hears. `IntersectionObserver` takes what it observes to be in view. A script that throws as it starts stops there, and the page stays, saying why. Python logic and code run in a worker are not given the document.

<Button variant="primary" size="md">Save</Button>
<Text>{message}</Text>
<Text color={isDark ? "white" : "black"}>{message}</Text>
blocks.caption: Literal properties and brace-delimited expressions.

blocks.text: Quoted values are literal strings. Braces hold expressions whose values come from the app’s state. Keep expressions simple and move complicated decisions into named logic functions.

blocks.code: Press to save, or read how. Total: {total} items
blocks.caption: Words and tags on one line keep the spaces between them; a quote inside a quoted value is written ".

blocks.text: Text is read the way HTML reads it. Within a line of words, a space between a word, a tag and an expression is a space on the page, and a run of spaces is one; the line breaks and indentation between tags written one to a line are layout and draw nothing. A space before a `#` that begins no block is kept: `Ticket {name} #{id}`. Entities such as `&`, `<`, `"` and ` ` are read in text and in a quoted value alike, so `"` writes the double quote a value is closed by. Inside braces the text is JavaScript, where a quote in a string is written `\"`.

An expression in braces is JavaScript’s expression syntax, read by SoftN rather than by the browser: comparisons, arithmetic, `?:`, `??`, member access, calls, array and object literals, template literals and arrow functions with a one-expression body, whose parameters may take their argument apart. It reads state and calls functions; statements belong in logic.

blocks.code:
<Text>{tasks.filter(t => !t.done).length} left</Text>
<Text>{Math.max(0, ...scores)}</Text>
<Text>{Object.entries(totals).map(([name, total]) => `${name}: ${total}`).join(", ")}</Text>
<Box style={{ ...cardStyle, opacity: busy ? 0.5 : 1 }} />
<Text>© {new Date().getFullYear()}</Text>
<Button @click={() => count++}>Add one</Button>
<Button @click={() => filters = { ...filters, [name]: !filters[name] }}>Toggle</Button>
{/* A comment in braces renders nothing. */}

rows: Parameters that take a value apart
`([key, value]) => key`, `({ id, title }) => title`, `({ size = "md" }) => size`, `(n, step = 1) => n + step`, `(first, ...others) => others.length`
A key that is worked out
One assignment or update in a handler
Numbers as JavaScript writes them (`12`, `2.5`, `.5`, `1e3`, `0xff`, `0b101`, `0o17`, `1_000`), strings, template literals, `true`, `false`, `null`, `undefined`
`new Date(…)`, `new Array(…)`, `new Map(…)`, `new Set(…)` and the `Intl` formatters (`new Intl.NumberFormat(…)`, `new Intl.DateTimeFormat(…)` and the rest), and nothing else
blocks.caption: The expression forms a template reads.

blocks.text: A variable can have any name JavaScript allows, including words markup also uses, such as `data`, `style`, `from` and `end`. A `function` expression, `async` and `await`, regular expression literals and a comma between two expressions are not read: the parser reports them, and the place for them is a logic function the expression calls. The bitwise operators and shifts (`&`, `|`, `^`, `~`, `<<`, `>>`, `>>>`) are read as in JavaScript, and `Intl` formats numbers and dates: `{new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", { style: "currency", currency: "USD" }).format(total)}`. An assignment or `++` changes state when a handler runs it. Written in the body of the page, as in `{count++}`, it would run every time the page is drawn, so there it is worth its value and changes nothing. In a handler, `items.push(x)`, `sort()`, `splice()` and the other methods that change the list they are called on change a list in state as an assignment does; where the page is drawn they work on a copy and state is unchanged.

blocks.title: Templates run beside the app, not inside its sandbox
blocks.text: Logic runs in the ZIPP sandbox. A template expression is evaluated by the host page, which is why it is limited to reading state, calling the app’s functions and the globals listed above.

blocks.code:
<Input :bind={username} placeholder="Enter your name" />
<Button @click={save}>Save</Button>
<Button @click={() => clear()}>Clear</Button>
blocks.caption: The username state and the save and clear functions are defined in the app’s logic.

blocks.text: `:bind` is two-way: what the person types is written back to the state variable. On a number field (`<input type="number">` or `<Input type="number">`) it writes a number while the field holds one, and `''` while it is empty or holds something that is not a number. On `<input type="range">` it gives a number, and on `<select multiple>` a list of the chosen values. Any other `:` property, such as `:value={x}`, only shows the value. A host that keeps a page’s state itself is handed the write in its place, through the `on<Name>Change(path, value)` or `onUpdate(path, value)` function it gave; a logic function of that name is an ordinary function, and `:bind` writes the variable as it always does. `@click` and the other `@` events call a handler. A handler may have a block body, `@click={() => { count++; save() }}`: its statements run one after another, each an expression of the kind markup reads; `if`, `let` and loops belong in a logic function. A logic call may be written where a handler needs its value, `@click={save(currentDraft())}`: it is waited for first, and if it fails the outer call is not made.

blocks.code:
<Button @click={() => adding = true}>New task</Button>
<Modal :bind={adding} title="New task">…</Modal>
<Confirm :bind={asking} title="Delete this task?" @confirm={() => remove(task)} />
<Tabs :bind={tab} tabs={[{ key: "open", label: "Open" }, { key: "done", label: "Done" }]} />
<Pagination :bind={page} totalPages={pages} />
blocks.caption: One variable is the dialog’s open state, the chosen tab or the current page; nothing else has to close the dialog.

blocks.text: `:bind` is also how a variable becomes a component’s own state when that state is not typed text. A `Modal`, `Drawer` or `Popover` is open while its variable is true and sets it false when the person closes it. A `Confirm` is shut by either answer, and `@confirm` still says which. `Tabs` holds the chosen tab’s key, `Pagination` the page, `Accordion` the keys of its open panels, and `Sidebar` whether it is collapsed. `<Toast :bind={saved}>` shows while `saved` is true and writes false when it closes. `<FileChooser :bind={files}>` keeps the chosen files, and an empty list when they are removed. A handler written beside the binding, such as `@close`, runs as well, after the variable is written. A handler written beside `:bind` reads the value just bound, however it is written: `@change={load(category)}` beside `:bind={category}` loads the category just chosen. A `DatePicker` holds the day as text, `"2026-10-12"`, and `null` once it is cleared; `Radio`, `Select` and `SegmentedControl` hold the chosen option’s own value, a number for a numbered option. A `Popover` with no `trigger` takes its first child as the trigger, so a button or an icon can open it: `<Popover :bind={open}><Button>Help</Button><Text>…</Text></Popover>`.

A handler bound by name receives an argument: for most events, a plain-data summary of the browser event, and for `@change` and `@input`, the new value. It is never the live DOM event: its `target` and `currentTarget` are data, what the element holds (`value`, `checked`, `name`, `dataset`), and `preventDefault()` can be called and does nothing, because the logic runs apart from the page; a modifier cancels a default. An arrow that names a parameter, `@keydown={(e) => e.key === "Enter" && add()}`, is given the same summary, with `e.preventDefault()` and `e.stopPropagation()` that act on the event, and `e.target` and `e.currentTarget` as records of what the element holds (`value`, `checked`, `dataset`, its size); that is not the live event either, and it leads to no element, document or window. On `@input` and `@change` a handler in braces is handed the new value, not the event, an arrow as well: `@input={(value) => search(value)}`; a handler in quotes, `@input="search(event.target.value)"`, is handed `event`. Write an arrow, `@click={() => save()}`, to call a function without it; Python apps need that form for functions with no parameters.

</form>
<Box className="backdrop" @click.self={() => close()}>
  <Card @click.stop={() => select(item)}>…</Card>
</Box>

blocks.text: `class:name={condition}` adds the class when the condition is true and nothing when it is not, alongside any `class` or `className` already written. `style:property={value}` sets a single CSS property, spelled as CSS spells it (`style:font-size`) or as a custom property (`style:--accent`). A value that is false, empty or missing sets nothing, so the stylesheet decides.

A class can also be written as a list or as a record of conditions: `className={["card", selected && "is-selected"]}` and `className={{ card: true, "is-selected": selected }}` both give the element `card`, and `is-selected` while `selected` holds. An `#empty` branch makes the first-run experience explicit, which is kinder than a blank area that leaves someone wondering whether the app has loaded. A header may leave out its parentheses, `#if isLoggedIn` or `#each task in tasks`, and then runs to the end of its line; `#else if` keeps them, since without them `#else` could not tell a condition from the words of its branch.

blocks.caption: A control bound to the loop item writes that row. The variable can take the item apart, and a loop can go through a record’s entries or a count.

blocks.text: `#each` goes through a list, a `Set`, a `Map` (as `[key, value]` pairs), a record (its values, with the key as the second name: `#each (value, key in settings)`) and a whole number, which counts from 1. Text is not gone through letter by letter. A second name after the variable is the index, or the key for a record, and `key={…}` after the header tells the page which row is which when the list is reordered. A `key={…}` that cannot be worked out for a row falls back to the row’s index, and the console says so. `of` reads as `in` does, as JavaScript’s `for…of` writes it: `#each (task of tasks)`.

Inside a loop over a list that is in the app’s state, `:bind={todo.done}` and an assignment such as `todo.done = true` write the row they are on. A `:bind` or an assignment may use any index: `answers[q.id]`, `todos[count - 1].done`. A write whose index is nothing is not made, and the console says so. Where the list is worked out in the page, as in `#each (todo in todos.filter(t => !t.done))`, or is a collection’s records, the item has no place in state to write to: nothing is written and the console says so. Change such an item in a logic function, by its id.

<import Header from="./components/header.ui" />
<import TodoItem from "./components/todo-item.ui" />
<logic src="./app.logic" />

<App>
  <Header />
  #each (todo in filteredTodos) key={todo.id}
    <TodoItem />
  #end

blocks.caption: A page imports another under a name and places it by that name. The `=` after `from` may be left out; both lines are read the same way.

blocks.code: toggleTodo(todo.id)} /> startEdit(todo.id)}>{todo.data.text}
blocks.caption: components/todo-item.ui, the page placed in the loop. `todo` is the loop’s variable, and `toggleTodo`, `startEdit` and `deleteTodo` are functions of the page that imports it.

blocks.text: An imported page is its content, placed. Wherever `<TodoItem />` is written, the markup of `todo-item.ui` is put in its place as if it had been typed there, so it is in the importing page’s scope: it reads that page’s state, calls that page’s functions, and inside an `#each` it sees the loop’s variable. A path is relative to the file that imports, and an imported page can import pages of its own.

Nothing written on the tag is passed to it. An imported page has no properties, events or children, so `<Header title="Tasks" />` places the header and leaves `title` behind, and the console says so: “<Header> is an imported page, so its attributes (title) are ignored.” Put what the page needs in state it can read. State that belongs to one row of a list, such as which row is being edited, lives in the page’s logic and is kept by the row’s id: the row’s markup is placed once for each item, and all of it reads the one scope.

items.description: Joins the importing page’s one logic block, ahead of that page’s own code. Its variables are the app’s: one of each, however many times the page is placed.

Its collections are declared for the whole document, once. One the main page already declares is not repeated, and where the two give one name to different collections the main page’s stands and the console names the other.
Its rules join the document’s one stylesheet, once however often the page is placed: after the main page’s own rules, in the order of the imports. A rule is not kept to the page it is written in.
A page that is one `<App>…</App>` and nothing else contributes what is inside it. The wrapper goes, with what was written on it: the app is the page that imports.

blocks.text: Use layout components for structure, display components for readable content and form components for actions and input. `asset("assets/cover.png")` resolves a file inside the bundle, and a section that repeats can be kept in a page of its own and imported where it is needed.

blocks.text: An app’s logic is JavaScript in `.logic` files or Python in `.py` files. Both run in ZIPP, an engine written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly for the browser. The file name decides the language, and an app uses one language for all its logic: a bundle that mixes them is refused. JavaScript logic is one classic script, sloppy unless it opens with `"use strict"` (comments may come before it), which then holds for all of it, in the browser and on the PHP and Rust hosts.

The engine runs the language; SoftN supplies the app integration: state, rendering and the host APIs it chooses to expose. Knowing JavaScript or Python does not mean every browser global, Node.js module, npm package or pip package is available.

blocks.text: A `$:` declaration is a name and the expression it is always worth: `$: remaining = tasks.filter(t => !t.done)`. A page, a function and another `$:` all read it as it stands. The values are worked out again before a page is drawn and before a function is called, each after the ones it reads, in whatever order they are written. A function that changes state and then reads one reads what it was when the function was called. An expression may go on over several lines where JavaScript would read it as one: a line that ends on an operator, or a next line that starts with `.`, `?`, `:` or an operator.

A function the page calls is followed the same way. `<Text>{label()}</Text>` is drawn again when any state `label` reads changes, directly or through the functions it calls, whether or not the page names that state. A function that only an event runs (`@click`, `@tick`, an `on…` prop) is not followed, so a game’s `tick` can work on large state without the page being told of every change. In JavaScript logic, `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `clearTimeout` and `clearInterval` work as in a browser, for a delay, a debounce or a countdown. A callback runs the way a click handler does, so what it writes is drawn, and every timer is cleared when the app stops. Set one from a logic function: markup cannot call them. A game clock is better as `<Loop frame running={running} @tick={step} />`, which calls `step(dt)` once for each frame the screen draws and stops while the app is hidden, or `<Loop interval={100} running={running} @tick={() => step()} />` for a timer. `requestAnimationFrame` waits about a frame (16 ms) before it calls its function, and hands it the time `performance.now()` reads.

    global tasks, draft
    title = draft.strip()
    if title == "":
        return
    tasks = tasks + [{"title": title, "done": False}]
    draft = ""
blocks.caption: Python: bind the input with :bind={draft} and the button with @click={() => add_task()}.

blocks.text: Both follow the same pattern: an action changes state explicitly, and the interface redraws from it. That is easier to trace than data changes hidden inside a display expression.

sections.title: The engine and the host are separate layers

blocks.text: ZIPP’s browser build is an interpreter inside WebAssembly. The upstream project’s native JIT tiers are not what runs in the browser, so native benchmark results are not SoftN browser performance.

The host decides what a script can call. Bridges such as `db` and `softn.*` are gated by the app’s declarations and the host’s grants, and a Python app’s calls go through the same checks. A bridge existing is no reason to assume unrestricted access.

blocks.title: The page is outside the guest
blocks.text: Logic is guest code in the environment the host gives it, not a script tag with access to the whole page.

A JavaScript syntax error is shown with the line it is on: `SyntaxError: unexpected token ';', at this line of the logic: let c = ;`. An error’s `stack` names the logic `logic` and counts lines from its first line, in the browser and on both backend hosts, so `at save (logic:12:5)` is line 12 of the logic. The logic is your logic files joined, with their imports inlined: for an app with one logic file, those are that file’s lines. A Python error names the module and the line it is in.

SoftN ships ZIPP v0.0.35’s javascript-python-base engine: JavaScript and Python in one WebAssembly module (6.58 MB, about 1.65 MB compressed), without torch. ZIPP’s verified torch package is installed beside it and loaded only for apps that declare torch. Neither is committed to the repository. `npm run fetch:zipp`, and the build and test scripts when it is missing, install the release named by the `zipp-vm` tag in `apps/softn-host-rust/Cargo.toml`, check it against that release’s SHA256SUMS and record its provenance in SOURCE.json.
Rebuilding the engine is a separate maintenance task with its own Rust and WebAssembly tooling; ordinary SoftN development never needs it.

The PHP and Rust hosts run server-side `.logic` as JavaScript. Python is for client logic: a `.py` file under `server/` would never run, and Studio’s validator says so. There are no timers in server logic: a request ends when its handler returns, so `setTimeout` and the others throw an error that says so.

sections.title: Learn the boundaries before adding integrations

blocks.text: Start with app state and records. When you add networking, media, GPU work or backend actions, read the relevant capability guide and test both the allowed and the denied path. A working expression proves less than a complete user flow.

pages.title: State, events and app lifecycle
pages.summary: Connect user actions to state, understand event data, and distinguish a running screen from durable records.

seo.title: State, events and app lifecycle | SoftN Docs
seo.description: SoftN state and events: handlers and the plain-data event they receive, two-way binding, keyboard and pointer input in JavaScript and Python, and state versus saved records.

sections.title: State connects behaviour to the interface

blocks.text: The top-level names in an app’s logic are its state. SoftN mirrors them into the renderer around each call into the logic, so a change made by an action shows up in every expression that reads it.

For a small app, keep important state obvious: a current filter, a form field, the records shown in a list or the selected item. Change it with named actions, so a click can be traced from the template to the function and back to the screen.

A handler bound by name, such as `@click={save}`, is called with whatever the component passes. For a browser event that is a plain-data summary: the type, pointer position and buttons, modifier keys, and `target` and `currentTarget` with what those elements hold (`value`, `checked`, `name`, `dataset`). It is never the live DOM event: `event.preventDefault()` can be called and does nothing, because the logic runs apart from the page. To cancel a default or act on one key, add a modifier to the event in the template: `@submit.prevent={save}`, `@keydown.enter={add}`. A `<form>` with no `action` never leaves its page.

`@change` and `@input` pass the new value instead. Other components pass their own data: DPad’s `@press` gives the direction and Slider’s `@change` the number. Check what the component you use passes before writing logic around it.

blocks.code:
<Input :bind={username} placeholder="Name" />
<Button @click={() => save()}>Save</Button>
blocks.caption: Read the bound username state inside save. The arrow calls save with no argument, which suits a Python function with no parameters.

blocks.text: For keys and pointers anywhere on the page, JavaScript logic uses `window.addEventListener` and Python logic uses `softn.on("keydown", handler)`. Either way the listener receives plain data, such as `key`, `code`, `clientX`, `clientY` and `targetTag`, not a browser object.
Box and Button forward pointerdown, pointerup, pointercancel and pointerleave, for controls that react while held. Handle cancellation and leaving the control, not only the first press.

blocks.code: softn.input.captureKeys(["ArrowUp", " ", "F1"])
blocks.caption: Keys the app captures from the page. The host still protects text fields, Ctrl with a character key (Ctrl+F, Ctrl+C) and the system modifier; Ctrl with an arrow or another named key is captured.

blocks.text: Capture only the keys the app needs. A game should not make it hard to type into its own settings form or use familiar browser shortcuts.

Calling `preventDefault()` on the record a window listener is given does nothing: logic hears a key after the browser has acted on it. The record’s `defaultPrevented` says whether the key was captured, and the first time a listener calls `preventDefault()` for a key that was not, the runtime says so in the console. For a game, `<Controls :bind={pad} keys={{ left: "ArrowLeft a", fire: "Space" }} />` does all of this: it keeps a record of what is held and captures exactly the keys it is given. See the guide to 3D scenes and games.

rows: Does the interface update after an action?
Does unfinished input survive returning Home and switching apps?
Does the data you meant to keep survive closing and reopening the app?
blocks.caption: Separate acceptance checks, not interchangeable definitions of persistence.

blocks.text: `_init()` runs once when the app loads, in either language. Use XDB for records: a counter or selected tab is not a database record. Decide which state should restart and which should be restored.

A permission allowed after the app opened takes effect in the running app, and `_init()` does not run again for it. Define `_onPermissionChange()` to do then what start-up could not: it is called when the app is allowed something more. An app that was refused something earlier and defines no `_onPermissionChange()` is started again instead, with its variables carried over and `_init()` run again, and so is any app a permission is taken away from. `_init()` also runs again when an editor’s preview takes a change to the logic, and not for a change to a page or its styles.

Define `_onHide()` and `_onShow()` to be told when the app goes to the background and when it comes back: another app chosen in a host that keeps several open, or the browser’s tab hidden and shown. A game pauses there, and a player stops its sound. An app that starts in the background is told `_onHide()` once, after `_init()`.

items.title: Check the function
items.text: Reduce it to one state change before adding database or network work. In Python, check the `global` line.

items.text: Permission, capability support and backend availability can fail independently of the UI.

items.text: Find out whether the problem appears after a redraw, an app switch, a close or a fresh open.

pages.title: SoftN component guide
pages.summary: Find a sensible starting component for layouts, forms, data, charts, media, animation and richer apps.

seo.title: SoftN component guide | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Explore SoftN components for layouts, forms, tables, dashboards, charts, media, animation, editors and Three.js scenes.

sections.title: Choose a component by the job it does

blocks.text: The built-in library is organised into layout, form, display, feedback, data, navigation, utility, chart, animation, editor, 3D and smart components. Start with the role you need rather than a list of every property.

This is a guide to finding a component, not a complete property reference. Every name below is registered in `@softn/components`; for exact properties and callback values, read a working example or the component’s source.

rows: App, Box, Stack, Grid, Card, Container, Layout, Header, Content, Section
Text, Heading, Badge, Tag, TagGroup, Avatar, AvatarGroup, Progress, Spinner, Skeleton, Image, Icon, Kbd
Button, ButtonGroup, CopyButton, Input, NumberInput, TextArea, Select, SegmentedControl, Checkbox, Radio, Switch, Rating, Form, Field, Slider
Alert, Modal, Confirm, Toast, Drawer, Popover, EmptyState
blocks.caption: A starting selection from the component library.

blocks.text: Choose the simplest component that matches the interaction. A small settings screen may need only a Stack, Heading, Input and Button. More components do not necessarily make the workflow clearer.

An `id` and any `data-…` or `aria-…` attribute written on a layout, text or button component (Box, Stack, Grid, Card, Container, Center, Text, Heading, Button, Badge, Tag, Icon, Image) is put on its element, so the page’s own `<style>` can find it: `<Box className="tool" data-on={tool === "wall"}>` with `.tool[data-on="true"] { … }`. Any other attribute a component does not know is dropped.

A `FileChooser` given `value` shows those files as chosen, and none for `[]`, so a page that keeps them can clear the chooser once they are sent; `disabled` turns it off, and nothing can be chosen, dropped or removed. Toasts shown at once at the same corner stack, the newest nearest the edge, and the older ones move back as the newer ones go.

rows: List, ListItem, Table, DataGrid, TreeView, Pagination
LineChart, BarChart, PieChart, AreaChart, RadarChart, GaugeChart
blocks.caption: Smart components offer data-driven configuration; ordinary components give you more direct presentation control.

blocks.text: Use a table when someone needs to inspect individual records. Use a chart for a question about a pattern or comparison. A chart is most useful when its labels, units and empty state make that question understandable.

Stat and Timeline draw what the app already holds in state: one figure with how it moved, and a list of things that happened. SmartStats and SmartTimeline are given what they draw too, and lay it out with less markup: SmartStats takes several figures in `stats`, as `label: value` pairs or a list of items, with `icons` and `trends` beside them; SmartTimeline takes records in `data`, a collection’s records included, and is told which of their fields hold each event’s `title`, `description`, `time` and `status`.

blocks.code:
<SegmentedControl :bind={view} options={["List", "Board", "Calendar"]} />
<NumberInput :bind={quantity} min={1} max={99} />
<Rating :bind={score} max={5} />
<Steps items={["Cart", "Shipping", "Payment"]} :bind={step} />
blocks.caption: Each binds like an Input: the state is shown, and what the person chooses is written back.

items.description: One choice from a few options shown side by side. `@change` and `:bind` give the option’s value. Use Tabs when the choice changes the page.
A number to type or to step with the buttons and the arrow keys, kept between `min` and `max`. It gives a number, or `null` when the field is empty, never the text.
A score out of `max` stars. With `readOnly` it shows a score and is read aloud as "3 out of 5".
Progress through a sequence. `current` is the step in progress, by position or by key; with `:bind` or `@change` the steps are buttons.

sections.title: Pieces you would otherwise lay out by hand

blocks.code:
<DescriptionList items={[{ label: "Customer", value: order.name }, { label: "Paid", value: order.paid }]} columns={2} />

<Field label="Volume" hint="Applies to every sound." error={volumeError}>
  <Slider :bind={volume} />
</Field>

<ButtonGroup ariaLabel="Range">
  <Button @click={() => range = "day"}>Day</Button>
  <Button @click={() => range = "week"}>Week</Button>
</ButtonGroup>

<CopyButton value={inviteLink} label="Copy invite" />

<Confirm open={asking} title="Delete this note?" message="This cannot be undone."
         confirmText="Delete" variant="danger"
         @confirm={() => remove()} @cancel={() => asking = false} />

<AvatarGroup max={3}>
  #each (person in people) key={person.id}
    <Avatar name={person.name} />
  #end
</AvatarGroup>
blocks.caption: Each of these replaces a layout that is otherwise written out again in every app.

items.description: The facts about one thing as labels and values. `items` is a list of `{ label, value, hint? }` or the record itself, whose keys become the labels. A value that is missing is shown as a dash, `true` and `false` as Yes and No, and `columns` falls to fewer on a narrow screen.

A label, a hint and an error around any control. Input, Select and TextArea carry their own; use Field for a Slider, a Rating, a SegmentedControl, a group of checkboxes or a control of your own. An `error` is shown in place of the hint and announced.
Buttons that belong together, joined edge to edge, or kept apart with `attached={false}`. For one choice of a few, SegmentedControl is the control.

A button that copies its `value` and says “Copied” for a moment, to the eye and to a screen reader, in place of a logic function, a state variable for the label and a timer. `iconOnly` shows the icon alone. In an app whose manifest denies it the clipboard, the button is disabled and says why.

A question with two answers, asked before something is done. The app keeps `open`: `@confirm` and `@cancel` tell it the answer, and it closes the dialog by changing `open`, so a failed action can leave the question up. `loading` holds both answers while the action runs.
A row of overlapping avatars with a count of those past `max`, and a row of tags that wraps. Put the Avatar or Tag tags inside, written out or from an `#each`.

blocks.text: The library also includes PixelGrid, PixelCanvas, QRCode, QRReader, Camera, Microphone, AudioStream, DPad and Controls; animation components such as AnimatedBox, AnimatedNumber, Sprite and TileMap; editors such as CodeEditor, MarkdownEditor and RichTextEditor; and Scene3D for Three.js scenes. Loop is the clock of a game, and Controls keeps what the player holds; the guide to 3D scenes and games shows them at work.

Their presence in the library does not remove browser constraints or host permissions. Media input and advanced host integrations should be checked in the actual deployment, not only in a component catalogue.
