pages.title: Forms, tables and dashboards
pages.summary: Build a useful record workflow before adding extra screens, summaries and visual polish.

seo.title: Forms, tables and dashboards | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Build SoftN forms, tables and dashboards with XDB, SmartForm, SmartGrid and clear record workflows, validation and empty states.

blocks.text: A record-oriented app usually needs a small loop: enter information, save it, show the result and update it later. Build that loop before adding several dashboards. It makes the relationship between the interface, logic and data easier to test.

SoftN offers ordinary form and data components, and smart components that configure themselves from a few attributes: SmartForm saves to a collection named by `collection`, while SmartGrid, SmartList and SmartCards draw the records they are given in `data`. Choose whichever makes your app’s behaviour easiest to explain.

blocks.code:
<SmartForm
  collection="clients"
  fields="name:text:required, email:email:required, phone:text"
  submitText="Add Client"
/>
blocks.caption: A SmartForm for a clients collection. The app supplies the collection.

blocks.text: The example identifies the collection and fields, including required name and email inputs. Treat validation at the UI as help for the user, not a substitute for checks on a private backend that accepts submitted data.

Once a new record is saved, the form says “Saved” for a moment and starts again from its `data` and `defaults`, ready for the next record, so a second press does not save the same record twice. `afterSave="keep"` leaves what was typed, for a similar next record, and `savedText` changes what the form says. A record being edited keeps its values. Use `@saved` for anything more: closing a dialog, or returning to a list.

blocks.code:
<data><collection name="clients" as="clients" /></data>

<SmartGrid
  data={clients}
  columns="name, email, phone, visits"
  searchable sortable pageable
/>
blocks.caption: A read-oriented SmartGrid. The page’s `<data>` binds the clients collection to `clients`, and SmartGrid draws the records it is given in `data`. Add editing only after defining and testing the update flow.

blocks.text: Choose columns for the task, not merely because the fields exist. Long text and too many columns can make a phone layout difficult. A list or card layout may be a better small-screen view.

sections.title: Add summaries that answer a question

blocks.text: SmartStats, chart components and ordinary display components can turn records into a dashboard. Give each summary a clear meaning: open tasks, visits during a period or records needing follow-up. Label the time window and units where they matter.
Compute summaries from the same intended records as the list. A dashboard and table that disagree may be using different filters, stale state or preview data instead of the live collection.

items: Start with no records and confirm the next action is clear.
Submit incomplete or invalid values and check the explanation.
Create a record and confirm it appears in the view.
Update a record and verify totals and filters still agree.
Reopen the app and check the intended persistence.
Check phone-sized layouts and keyboard access.

blocks.text: When the flow needs shared authenticated records, add a backend deliberately. Local XDB storage and server authorisation solve different problems.

pages.title: Local app data with XDB
pages.summary: Understand collections, record operations, seeds, app identity and optional synchronisation.

seo.title: Local app data with XDB | SoftN Docs
seo.description: XDB in SoftN: local collections, the synchronous db bridge, bundle seeds, app-scoped storage, host-dependent sync, and what Python apps use instead of db.

blocks.text: XDB is SoftN’s local-first data layer. It keeps app-scoped records and gives JavaScript logic a `db` bridge with synchronous operations over an in-memory cache; how records persist, and whether native storage is used, depends on the host.
Think of a collection as records of one kind, such as clients or tasks. Think separately about its schema, its starting seed records and the live records someone creates while using the app.

blocks.title: Python apps
blocks.text: `db` is a JavaScript global. Python logic has no `db`, so it cannot read or write the app’s local records. It can use `softn.storage.*` (Server storage, below), which keeps records on the server and answers only in an app opened from the directory that publishes it.

blocks.caption: Create, query, update and delete. Skip the last line if you want to keep the record.

blocks.text: Create and query name a collection; update and delete take a record id. The full `db` surface:

items.description: One record, or null when it does not exist.
The records of a collection, optionally those matching the given field values.
Adds a record and returns it with its id.

Merges the patch into the record and returns the result. A record that is not there, deleted or never created, is an error the script can catch, on the page’s thread and in a worker alike; `db.get` first if it may be gone.
Marks the record deleted, so sync peers learn about it.
Removes the record outright, without a tombstone. There is no call that empties a collection or keeps only its newest records: query the records and remove each one.

Optional peer synchronisation; see below. `options` reach the room from a `.ui` page's script; from `.logic`, `db.startSync` takes the room alone and returns nothing. `db.getSavedSyncRoom()` names the room the app last started and has not stopped, or is null.

blocks.text: For a reactive screen, make it clear when the state the UI shows is refreshed. The usual pattern queries records in `_init()` and queries again after each change.

Builder’s Data view shows each collection’s structure and seed records. Use the schema to make field intent clear, and ship only seeds that suit every recipient. Do not distribute a real customer dataset because it made a convincing local demo.

blocks.title: Preview is not the exported database
blocks.text: Builder’s preview has its own test records. Review the seeds in the Data view and test a fresh app instance before assuming the export holds the intended starting data.

sections.title: App identity is not just a display name

blocks.text: The general loader isolates bundles by digest, while single-app and FormLogic hosts provide their own identity. A display name alone is no authority to read another app’s data.
Treat upgrades and moves between hosts as data-lifecycle decisions. Before changing an identity or deployment, test which records remain available and keep a recovery copy suited to that host.

blocks.code: db.startSync('my-room-name')
blocks.caption: Start peer synchronisation. The host must support it and the app needs the sync capability.

blocks.text: A room name is not an authentication or privacy policy. Decide who may take part, how access is controlled and what the host provides before using sync for sensitive or multi-user records.

What a room carries and who can read it: a room carries every collection of the app whose name does not start with `_`, not only the ones a game or a lobby uses, unless `permission.json` names them. With `"sync": { "enabled": true, "roomCollections": ["scores"] }` every room of the app carries `scores` alone, both ways: nothing else is sent, and nothing a peer puts in another collection is written here. From logic, `db.startSync` takes the room alone, so the declaration is how a logic app limits its rooms. A room that has carried other collections keeps them in its shared document, here and on its peers, so start a new room for a narrower list. A shared room's key is worked out from its name, so anyone who knows the name can read and write it, the signalling server that introduces the peers included. A private room's name is its key: it is joined under a name worked out from it, so the signalling server never sees it, and what it sends to find its peers is encrypted with it, so only a device that knows the name can join. A private room is then as private as its name is hard to guess, so make it long and random, as an invitation code is, never a word or a person's name. On a page served over plain HTTP from another machine the browser withholds the encryption this needs, and a private room is joined under its name as before; the console says so. Keep what must stay on one device in a collection whose name starts with `_`.

Peer sync runs while the app is on screen. Where a host keeps several apps open, as SoftN Web’s tabs do, an app’s rooms wait while another app is shown: nothing arrives from its peers and nothing is sent, and what the app writes meanwhile is exchanged when it is shown again. Closing the app leaves its rooms, and `db.getSavedSyncRoom()` still names the last one, so the app can start it again when it next opens. Sync through the server the manifest names (`config.server.url`) is live while the app is shown; behind another app it keeps its connection only while there is something of its own to send, and for half a minute after, so what it writes meanwhile still reaches the server and what others changed arrives when it is shown again. The server, its token and the collections it carries are set in the manifest’s `config.server` (see the app format guide), and server sync, like peer sync, needs the `sync` declaration and the person’s Allow.
Local persistence, peer-to-peer sync and a private server database are not interchangeable. Choose the one that matches the app’s ownership, sharing and recovery needs.

`softn.storage` keeps an app’s records in a database of its own on the app directory that published it, shared by everyone who runs the app. It answers only in an app opened from that directory: from its listing in SoftN Web, or on its `/play/<slug>` page. Anywhere else (a Builder or Studio preview, a `.softn` file opened in SoftN Web, the desktop runtime, a single-app site) every call answers `{ error: "This app has no server storage: it was not opened from a directory that publishes it." }`. The app also needs the `storage` capability.

blocks.caption: Add a score, then read the ten highest. A query answers { records, total, limit, offset }, and each record is { id, data, createdAt, updatedAt, mine }.

blocks.text: Every call ends with a callback, which receives the result or `{ error }`: `insert(collection, data)`, `get(collection, id)`, `update(collection, id, data)`, `set(collection, id, data)`, `remove(collection, id)`, `query(collection, { where, orderBy, limit, offset })`, `count(collection, where)`, `collections()` and `clear(collection)`, and `kvGet(key)`, `kvSet(key, value)` and `kvRemove(key)` for plain keys. Python calls the same functions after `import softn`, the last three also as `kv_get`, `kv_set` and `kv_remove`.

Who may do what to a collection is its policy, declared in `permission.json` and fixed when the app is published: `"storage": { "enabled": true, "collections": { "scores": "append-only", "*": "public" } }`. `public` is the default: anyone running the app can read, change and remove every record. `append-only` lets anyone add and read, and only the publisher change or remove. `owner-write` lets anyone read, and a record is changed or removed only by whoever added it, or the publisher. `private` shows each visitor only the records they added. `publisher` needs the app’s edit key, which the app cannot reach from a visitor. `*` sets the policy for every collection not named, and the plain keys have no policy: they are always public.

items.label: Per-app storage, in the directory guide
items.description: The route each call becomes, the policies and the visitor token that says who added a record.

pages.title: Assets, themes and responsive layouts
pages.summary: Keep an app readable, portable and testable across sizes without relying on your own browser cache.

seo.title: Assets, themes and responsive layouts | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Manage SoftN assets, light and dark themes, and responsive layouts. Test exported bundles, narrow screens and fresh app instances.

sections.title: Keep distributable assets with the app

blocks.text: A bundle’s `assets/` folder holds images, styles, sounds, models and other resources. In markup, `asset()` resolves a path inside the bundle, and the audio API resolves bundle paths the same way.

A local file that exists only on your development machine is not automatically part of the exported app. Reopen the exported bundle in a fresh context to catch missing resources that your current preview or browser cache may hide.

blocks.code: <Image src={asset("assets/cover.png")} alt="The book’s cover" />
blocks.caption: The asset helper with an Image component. Include the file in the app.

sections.title: Design for the theme you support

blocks.text: The App component takes a `theme`, and Builder’s new projects offer Light, Dark or System. Fieldnotes shows one app drawn in both palettes, and the runtime switches theme without clearing unfinished input.
Three things can say whether an app is light or dark, and the first one that does decides:

items: The page. `<App theme="light">` or `<App theme="dark">` is that side wherever it runs. The word can be written or worked out, as in `theme={darkMode ? "dark" : "light"}`, which is how an app offers a switch of its own.

The project. Builder saves the project’s Light or Dark as `config.theme.mode` in `manifest.json`, and the web runtime, a single-app page, the desktop runtime and FormLogic, for an app embedded there, all draw the app on that side, over the host’s own theme and the visitor’s device.

The host, for a project set to System or with no mode: softn.com’s theme in the web runtime, the desktop runtime’s own theme, the deployment’s `theme` on a single-app page, and FormLogic’s theme for an app embedded there.

blocks.text: Components take their colours from the side that was chosen, chart series and code colours included. Where that side is not the host’s own, the app is also given a ground and a text colour of its side, so an app with no `<App>` does not stand on the host’s page. One case is kept as it always was: in a project set to System, a page that pins its own theme has its own colours, while chart and code colours go on following the host. Set the project to Light or Dark and they follow the page.

Test your own colours in each supported theme. A hard-coded text colour that works on one background can become unreadable on another. Use meaning, labels and shape as well as colour to communicate status.

sections.title: A preview size is a test case

blocks.text: Builder previews Desktop, Tablet and Mobile sizes, but responsive behaviour is still part of the layout you wrote. Switching size does not redesign a row of buttons with too many items or a panel with a fixed width.

items: Check the narrowest screen you intend to support.
Try long headings, validation messages and realistic record values.
Keep important controls reachable without horizontal scrolling.
Check how charts and tables behave when their container shrinks.
Test the actual interaction after a theme or viewport change.

blocks.code:
<Grid columns={3} gap="md" collapseOnMobile>…</Grid>
<Grid columns={{ sm: 1, md: 2, lg: 4 }} gap="md">…</Grid>
<Grid minColumnWidth="220px" gap="md">…</Grid>
<Stack direction="horizontal" gap="md" mobileVertical>…</Stack>
blocks.caption: Layouts that change with the width of the screen, without a stylesheet.

blocks.text: A Grid with a plain `columns={3}` keeps three columns at every width, which is what a keypad or a game board needs. `collapseOnMobile` makes it one column below 768 pixels, a `columns` object names a count for each width, and `minColumnWidth` fits as many columns as have that much room. A horizontal Stack with `mobileVertical` becomes a column on a phone.

Some components change by themselves. At 768 pixels and under a `Sidebar` is a menu button, in a slim bar where the sidebar stood, that opens it over the page as a drawer; choosing a NavItem or a link in it closes it. `menuLabel` names the button, and the drawer it opens, for a screen reader, and is “Menu” when left out. An app that draws its own phone navigation gets no second one: an element with the `softn-mobile-only` class, or a menu button of its own (a control named “Menu” or “Open menu”), is taken for that, and `mobileMenu={false}` says so outright. At 640 pixels and under a `Table` too wide for its box draws each row as a card, as SmartGrid does: `mobileCards="never"` keeps it a table that scrolls sideways, and `"always"` draws cards whatever its width. `Tabs` that do not fit scroll in their own row. Under a finger, controls that are compact for a mouse are 44 pixels tall.

A remote image, font, audio file or model makes the app depend on a network service even when its records are local. Decide whether the asset should be bundled, fetched when needed or treated as optional.

For an app that must work offline, test after the host reports the saved app ready, then disable the connection and exercise the real workflow. The word local-first does not automatically package a remote resource.

pages.summary: A readable map of the interface, guest logic, data and hosting responsibilities.

seo.title: How SoftN, ZIPP and XDB fit together | SoftN Docs
seo.description: SoftN architecture: .ui rendered through React, JavaScript or Python logic in the ZIPP WebAssembly engine, the source composer, XDB records and optional backend hosts.

sections.title: A small map of the platform

blocks.text: SoftN connects an editable UI language, application logic and records. It is easiest to understand with the renderer, the script engine, the database and the host kept as separate responsibilities.

blocks.code:
Editable .softn client bundle
  |
  +-- .ui source ----------> SoftN parser / renderer --> React interface
  |
  +-- .logic or .py -------> ZIPP (WebAssembly) -------> app behaviour
  |
  +-- XDB seeds and assets

The source composer checks and joins the pieces before anything runs.
Host integration connects behaviour to app-scoped records
and to explicitly supported, granted capabilities.

Optional private backend
  authenticated actions --> server logic (JavaScript) / server database
blocks.caption: A responsibility map. A backend is separate from the public client download.

blocks.text: A lexer, parser and renderer turn `.ui` source into React elements through a component registry. Properties and template expressions connect the visible interface to the app’s state.
Authors work in SoftN’s source format. React is part of the host’s rendering, not a separate React project every app author maintains.

Before an app runs, the source composer resolves each page’s `<logic src>`, decides the language from the file names and checks the rules: one language per app, Python in files, valid and unique module names, declared packages. Builder’s preview, Studio’s preview and validator, and Runtime all use the same composer, so a refusal appears in the editor before Run.

ZIPP compiles JavaScript or Python to register bytecode and runs it. In the browser, the WebAssembly build uses its interpreter rather than the native JIT tiers. SoftN’s engine is ZIPP’s javascript-python-base build, which carries both languages in one module, with torch added as a separate package only when an app declares it; a JavaScript app and a Python app use separate engine instances.

SoftN mirrors the logic’s top-level state into the renderer around each call and supplies host bridges. That is why a button handler can change a variable and redraw an expression without receiving access to the whole browser environment.

XDB supplies app-scoped local records. Bundle seeds provide starting content, while the host controls persistence and identity. Optional sync and native storage depend on what the host supports and allows.
A private SQLite database on a server is a different resource with different access rules. A client can request named backend operations without receiving that database or its credentials.

Builder, Studio and Runtime work with the same editable bundle, while a browser, the desktop loader or a configured website provides the execution environment. FormLogic is an optional connected host with its own authenticated backend.

blocks.title: A shared engine is not shared authority
blocks.text: Hosts can reuse verified engine bytes while each worker or app keeps its own instance, memory and permissions. Reusing an artifact does not share a running VM or grant access between apps.

seo.title: Audio, microphone and media | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Use audio and media in SoftN: sound playback from logic, browser autoplay rules, microphone and camera permissions, and how to test them.

blocks.text: Logic plays sound with `softn.audio`, in JavaScript or, after `import softn`, in Python. Asset paths are resolved inside the bundle. Playback is not microphone capture: playing a bundled sound reads nothing from the microphone.

blocks.caption: Playback calls in JavaScript. Declare themeHandle in your app state and include both audio files.

blocks.text: `setVolume` scales current and later playback, and `whenEnded(handle, callback)` reports when a sound finishes. The runtime stops the audio an app started when that app closes.

Browsers can refuse playback before the person interacts with the page. A one-shot sound then reports `played: false` and `blocked: true`. A looped track reports `pending: true` with its handle and starts on the first click or keystroke.
Design the first screen so sound is optional rather than the only explanation of what is happening. A visible Start action is easier to understand than an app that depends on immediate audio.

blocks.title: Test on a fresh page
blocks.text: A browser that has already received your clicks is not a useful test of the first-visit autoplay path.

sections.title: Microphone and camera are different permissions

blocks.text: The component library includes Camera, Microphone and AudioStream. Capture needs host support and the camera or mic capability, and the browser may also ask the person for consent.
The audio playback API is not permission-gated in the same way as microphone capture. Do not broaden an app’s requested capabilities merely to play a bundled sound effect.

blocks.title: Ask only when the feature needs it
blocks.text: Explain what capture is for and provide a useful denied-permission state. Do not silently upload captured material or embed private service credentials in the client.

items: Try a fresh session before any interaction.
Try permission denial and a device without the requested input.
Check that playback and capture stop at the intended point.
Check volume, mute behaviour and visible feedback.
Try the browser and host you plan to support, not only the development preview.

blocks.text: Capture callbacks and speech APIs are beyond this introduction. See the repository’s media and local-speech notes for the version you deploy.

pages.title: 3D scenes and games with SoftN
pages.summary: Write a game or an interactive 3D scene as a page: a loop on the screen’s frames, what the player holds as one record, and objects as a list. With five complete examples that SoftN’s tests play, what makes a scene look real, and how to play a scene made in Blender.

seo.title: 3D scenes and games with SoftN | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Build games and interactive 3D scenes in SoftN: a frame loop with dt, keys, gamepad and touch as one record, Scene3D objects, a follow camera, scenes made in Blender, and five tested examples.

sections.title: What a game is made of

blocks.text: A game in SoftN is a page like any other. Its state is the top-level variables of its logic, the page draws from them, and a loop calls one function again and again to move things on. Four pieces do the work, and each is a tag or a function you can copy from the examples below.

rows: Calls `step(dt)` once for each frame the screen draws, with `dt` the seconds since the last call. It stops while nobody can see the app.
Keeps a record of what the player holds: `pad.left` is true while held, `pad.presses.fire` counts presses. Keys, a gamepad and an on-screen `<DPad :bind={pad} />` write the same record.
Plain elements or an `<svg>` under `#each`, `<Sprite>`, `<TileMap>`, `<PixelGrid>`, `<PixelCanvas>`, or `<Scene3D>`
Draws the state. The score, the menus and the buttons are ordinary markup over or beside it.
Called when the app goes to the background and when it comes back, so a game can pause and a sound can stop.
blocks.caption: The four pieces of a game. None needs a permission.

blocks.text: Logic is modern JavaScript: classes, spread, destructuring, `for…of`, arrow functions, typed arrays, generators and `async`/`await` all work. Keep each thing in the game as a small record in a list, and write movement as a speed multiplied by `dt`.
Dodge the falling rocks. Move with the arrow keys or A and D, with a gamepad, or with the pad on screen; Space or Enter starts. The whole game is one file: the logic first, then the page.

blocks.code:
// Dodge: slide left and right, and let the rocks go past. let W = 320 let H = 440 let pad = { presses: {} } // what the player holds; and keep it let player = { x: 140, y: 400, w: 40, h: 16 } let rocks = [] let score = 0 let best = 0 let playing = false let paused = false let over = false let nextId = 1 let spawnIn = 0 function _init() { best = Number(localStorage.getItem("dodge:best")) || 0 } function start() { if (!paused) { rocks = [] score = 0 spawnIn = 0 player.x = (W - player.w) / 2 } over = false paused = false playing = true } // Two boxes overlap when neither is wholly to one side of the other. function overlaps(a, b) { return a.x < b.x + b.w && a.x + a.w > b.x && a.y < b.y + b.h && a.y + a.h > b.y } // One step of the game. dt is the seconds since the last step, so every // speed is in pixels a second and the game runs the same on any screen. function step(dt) { const direction = (pad.right ? 1 : 0) - (pad.left ? 1 : 0) player.x = Math.max(0, Math.min(W - player.w, player.x + direction * 240 * dt)) spawnIn -= dt if (spawnIn <= 0) { rocks.push({ id: nextId++, x: Math.random() * (W - 20), y: -20, w: 20, h: 20, speed: 120 + Math.random() * 140 }) spawnIn = 0.45 } for (const rock of rocks) rock.y += rock.speed * dt if (rocks.some(rock => overlaps(rock, player))) { playing = false over = true if (score > best) { best = score localStorage.setItem("dodge:best", String(best)) } return } const before = rocks.length rocks = rocks.filter(rock => rock.y < H) score += before - rocks.length } // calls this once for each press of an action, by its name. function pressed(action) { if (action === "start" && !playing) start() } // The app went to the background: nobody can see the rocks coming. function _onHide() { if (playing) { playing = false paused = true } } Dodge Score {score} · Best {best}
#each (rock in rocks) key={rock.id}
#end #if (!playing)
{over ? "Hit! Press Space to play again" : paused ? "Paused. Press Space to go on" : "Press Space to start"}
#end
blocks.caption: A complete 2D game. This is docs/examples/game-dodge.ui, which SoftN’s tests play: they start it with Space, hold the right arrow, check that the page did not scroll, put the app in the background and see the game pause itself.

items: The rocks and the player are plain `<div>` elements placed with `style:left` and `style:top`, one for each record under `#each`. That is enough for dozens of moving things. Give each record an `id` and the loop a `key`, so an element follows its rock.
`step(dt)` moves everything by its speed times `dt`. On a 60 Hz screen `dt` is about 0.016, on a 120 Hz screen about 0.008, and the game runs at the same speed on both.
The score, the best score and the banner are ordinary markup that reads the same variables. `localStorage` keeps the best score for this app.
Changing `player.x` in place and pushing to `rocks` is seen by the page: after each call the runtime notices what changed.

blocks.code: <Loop frame running={playing} @tick={step} />
blocks.caption: One call of `step` for each frame, while `playing` is true. From docs/examples/game-dodge.ui.

blocks.text: `<Loop frame>` follows the screen: one `@tick` for each frame it draws, never a second one while the first is still running, and none while the app or the browser’s tab is hidden. The first tick after it is shown again is handed one frame’s time, not the time it was away, and no tick is ever handed more than 0.2 seconds. `maxFps={30}` caps the rate for logic too heavy to run on every frame.

Without `frame`, a Loop is a timer: `<Loop interval={100} running={running} @tick={step} />` calls every 100 milliseconds, whatever the screen is doing, and goes on in the background unless you add `pauseHidden`. Use the timer for a turn-based clock or a countdown, and `frame` for anything that moves.

blocks.title: Always multiply by dt
blocks.text: Do not assume a fixed step such as 0.033. A tick may be late, a screen may be faster than another, and when the logic is behind, a tick is skipped rather than queued: the next one is handed the longer `dt`. Movement written as speed times `dt` is right in every case.

A call made by `@tick` is one the runtime may leave out when the logic cannot keep up, as it may a call from the pointer moving (`@pointermove`, `@mousemove`, `@touchmove`, `@hover`), from `@scroll`, `@wheel`, `@drag`, `@dragover` and `@timeupdate`, and from a component’s meters (`@level`, `@fps`, `@frame`): the next one says the same thing later. A call from `@click`, a key, `@change`, `@submit`, `@press` or any other event is never left out, whatever the function is called.

blocks.code: <Controls :bind={pad} keys={{ left: "ArrowLeft a", right: "ArrowRight d", start: "Space Enter" }} @press={pressed} />
blocks.caption: The actions of the game and the keys that hold each. From docs/examples/game-dodge.ui.

blocks.text: `<Controls>` draws nothing. It keeps the variable it is bound to as a record: each action by its name, true while it is held, and `presses`, which counts how many times each has gone down. Start the variable as `{ presses: {} }`; the component fills in the rest.

items: A key is named as the browser names it, by `key` or by `code`: `"ArrowLeft"`, `"a"`, `"Space"`, `"Enter"`, `"ShiftLeft"`. Several keys for one action are separated by spaces.
The keys you name are kept from the browser while the app has the keyboard, so the arrows and Space do not scroll the page. Keys typed into a field, and the browser’s own shortcuts, are left alone.
Everything is let go when the window loses focus, when the app or the tab is hidden, and when the component is taken off the page. `enabled={false}` does the same while a menu is open.

A connected gamepad holds the same actions: its left stick and its d-pad hold the actions named `left`, `right`, `up` and `down`, and its buttons hold the other actions in the order `keys` lists them. `gamepad={{ fire: 0 }}` names the buttons yourself, and `gamepad={false}` reads none.
`<DPad :bind={pad} />` writes `left`, `right`, `up` and `down` into the same record, so touch needs no code of its own.

To act once on a press rather than while a key is held, either compare the count (`if (pad.presses.fire > fired) { fired = pad.presses.fire; shoot() }`) or use `@press={pressed}`, which calls your function once for each press with the action’s name.

blocks.text: You can still listen on the window yourself: `window.addEventListener("keydown", onKey)` hands `onKey` a plain record with `key`, `code`, `repeat` and the modifier keys. Two rules apply there. Calling `e.preventDefault()` in such a listener does nothing, because logic hears a key after the browser has acted on it; the runtime says so once in the console. To keep keys from the browser, name them first with `softn.input.captureKeys(["ArrowUp", " "])`, after which the record’s `defaultPrevented` is true for them.

blocks.caption: The whole of a collision between two boxes. From docs/examples/game-dodge.ui, where `step` asks it of every rock and the player.

blocks.text: There is no physics engine to learn. For boxes, the four comparisons above are the whole test; for round things, compare the distance between the centres with the sum of the radii, as the 3D game below does with `Math.hypot`. Test after moving, in the same `step`, and change the score in the same place.

rows: Plain elements, or shapes in an `<svg>`, one for each record under `#each`, as the example does
A character from a sheet of frames
`<Sprite src={asset("assets/hero.png")} x={hero.x} y={hero.y} flipX={hero.facingLeft} frames={[4, 5, 6]} />`. With `loop={false}` the frames play once and `@end` is called
Every pixel, sixty times a second
blocks.caption: Start with plain elements. Move to a specialist component when the game needs what it does.

blocks.text: A sprite’s `x` and `y` are pixels from the corner of its container, so give the playing field `position: relative`. `frames` counts along the sheet from the first frame of the sprite’s `row`, and `flipX` turns a walk drawn facing right to face left. A file in the app’s bundle is named in the page with `asset("assets/hero.png")`; `softn.audio.play("assets/sfx/hit.wav")` plays one from logic.

sections.title: A page with an interactive 3D scene

blocks.text: `<Scene3D>` draws a list of records. Logic never touches Three.js: it keeps the list, and the scene draws it. This page shows three parts of a plant; a click on one lights it up, and its reading appears over it, in the scene.

blocks.code:
// The parts of a small plant. Each is one record: what to draw, and what to say of it. let parts = [ { id: "pump", name: "Pump", note: "1450 rpm", type: "cylinder", radius: 0.5, height: 1.2, color: "#3b82f6", position: { x: -2, y: 0.6, z: 0 } }, { id: "valve", name: "Valve", note: "Open 40%", type: "torus", radius: 0.5, color: "#f59e0b", position: { x: 0, y: 0.6, z: 0 }, animate: { rotateY: 0.01 } }, { id: "tank", name: "Tank", note: "62% full", type: "capsule", radius: 0.6, height: 2, color: "#10b981", position: { x: 2, y: 1, z: 0 } } ] // The ground is scenery, not a part: a click on it is a click on nothing. let ground = { id: "ground", type: "plane", width: 12, height: 12, rotation: { x: -Math.PI / 2, y: 0, z: 0 }, color: "#1f2937", pickable: false } // The lights: a soft one from everywhere, and a sun. let lights = [ { type: "ambient", intensity: 0.6 }, { type: "directional", intensity: 1.2, position: { x: 4, y: 8, z: 5 } } ] let selectedId = "" $: selected = parts.find(part => part.id === selectedId) // What the scene draws: every part, the chosen one lit from within and a little larger, and the ground. $: objects = parts.map(part => ({ ...part, emissive: part.id === selectedId ? part.color : "#000000", emissiveIntensity: part.id === selectedId ? 0.6 : 0, scale: part.id === selectedId ? 1.15 : 1 })).concat([ground]) // A click on a part says which one. function pick(hit) { selectedId = hit.objectId } // A click on nothing, and Close, put the reading away. function close() { selectedId = "" } Plant overview Drag to look around. Click a part for its reading.
#if (selected) {selected.note} #end
blocks.caption: A page with a 3D scene. This is docs/examples/scene-parts.ui, which SoftN’s tests run: they click the valve and the tank, click on nothing, and read the card each time.

items: An object is a record with an `id` and a `type`: a shape such as `"box"`, `"sphere"`, `"cylinder"`, `"capsule"`, `"cone"`, `"torus"` or `"plane"`, or `"model"`, `"instanced"`, `"group"` or `"particles"`. `position`, `rotation` (in radians), `scale` and `color` place and paint it.

Give the scene its lights as a list too: an `"ambient"` light for the shade and a `"directional"` one for the sun is a good start. A scene given no lights at all is lit with those two, so a first scene is never black.

`@click` hands your function what was hit: `hit.objectId` is the object’s `id`. `@miss` is a click on nothing. The ground says `pickable: false`, so a click on it is a click on nothing too, and puts the card away.

`<SceneAnchor object={id}>` inside the scene holds ordinary markup over that object: a name, a reading, a card with a button. The scene keeps it there as the object and the camera move, and hides it when its place is out of view. `offset` lifts it clear of the object; `place="above"` sits it over the pin.
`transition={250}` takes an object to its new size, place, turn and colour over a quarter of a second instead of at once: the chosen part grows and lights up, it does not jump.
`animate: { rotateY: 0.01 }` is motion the scene keeps up itself, with no tick from logic.
`fill` sizes the scene to the box it is in, and `orbitControls` lets the person turn the view by dragging. `orbit` says how far: no nearer than 4, no farther than 14, and not under the ground.

blocks.text: Ask Studio’s assistant, or read the component reference, for every field of an object, a light, a hit and the effects: the reference is generated from the component’s own source and lists each with its meaning and its unit.
The same pieces make a 3D game: a Loop, Controls, and a scene. `pointerLock` gives the scene the mouse for looking around, and logic reads where it looks.

blocks.code:
// Walk: look with the mouse, move with W A S D or the arrows, pick up the coins. let pad = { presses: {} } let me = { x: 0, z: -6 } let coins = [] let found = 0 let playing = false let held = false // whether the scene has held the pointer in this run let camera = { position: { x: 0, y: 1.6, z: -6 }, fov: 70 } let objects = [] // What never changes is kept apart from what moves, so it is sent to the scene once. let scenery = [ { id: "ground", type: "plane", width: 40, height: 40, rotation: { x: -Math.PI / 2, y: 0, z: 0 }, color: "#14532d" }, { id: "north", type: "box", width: 40, height: 3, depth: 0.5, position: { x: 0, y: 1.5, z: 20 }, color: "#57534e" }, { id: "south", type: "box", width: 40, height: 3, depth: 0.5, position: { x: 0, y: 1.5, z: -20 }, color: "#57534e" }, { id: "east", type: "box", width: 0.5, height: 3, depth: 40, position: { x: 20, y: 1.5, z: 0 }, color: "#57534e" }, { id: "west", type: "box", width: 0.5, height: 3, depth: 40, position: { x: -20, y: 1.5, z: 0 }, color: "#57534e" } ] let lights = [ { type: "hemisphere", intensity: 0.9, color: "#bfdbfe", groundColor: "#14532d" }, { type: "directional", intensity: 1, position: { x: 6, y: 10, z: 4 } } ] function scatter() { coins = [ { id: "coin-1", x: -4, z: -2 }, { id: "coin-2", x: 3, z: 0 }, { id: "coin-3", x: -2, z: 4 }, { id: "coin-4", x: 5, z: 6 } ] found = 0 me = { x: 0, z: -6 } } // The lists the scene draws from, made again after each step. function draw() { camera = { position: { x: me.x, y: 1.6, z: me.z }, fov: 70 } objects = coins.map(coin => ({ id: coin.id, type: "torus", radius: 0.35, tube: 0.1, color: "#fbbf24", emissive: "#f59e0b", emissiveIntensity: 0.4, position: { x: coin.x, y: 1, z: coin.z }, animate: { rotateY: 0.05 } // the scene spins it; logic does not })) } function _init() { scatter() draw() } // From the Start button: a click is when a browser lets a page take the pointer. function start() { if (coins.length === 0) { // A new game: the coins again, facing the way the first one began. scatter() softn.scene.yaw = 0 softn.scene.pitch = 0 } softn.scene.lock() held = false playing = true draw() } function step(dt) { // Escape gives the pointer back. The scene says so, and the game waits. if (softn.scene.locked) held = true else if (held) { playing = false return } // On the ground the camera faces (sin yaw, cos yaw), and its right is (-cos yaw, sin yaw). const yaw = softn.scene.yaw const forward = (pad.forward ? 1 : 0) - (pad.back ? 1 : 0) const right = (pad.right ? 1 : 0) - (pad.left ? 1 : 0) me.x += (Math.sin(yaw) * forward - Math.cos(yaw) * right) * 4 * dt me.z += (Math.cos(yaw) * forward + Math.sin(yaw) * right) * 4 * dt me.x = Math.max(-19, Math.min(19, me.x)) me.z = Math.max(-19, Math.min(19, me.z)) // A coin is picked up when the player is within reach of it. const before = coins.length coins = coins.filter(coin => Math.hypot(coin.x - me.x, coin.z - me.z) > 0.9) found += before - coins.length if (coins.length === 0) { playing = false softn.scene.unlock() } draw() } function _onHide() { if (playing) { playing = false softn.scene.unlock() } }
{found} of 4 coins
#if (!playing)
Mouse to look, W A S D to walk, Esc to stop
#end
blocks.caption: A first-person game. This is docs/examples/game-walk.ui, which SoftN’s tests play: they press Start, check the scene was asked for the pointer, walk forward, turn, and let the pointer go.

items.description: Which way the scene’s camera faces, in radians. Read them to move the player that way; set them to turn the camera for a new game or a teleport. On the ground the camera faces (sin yaw, cos yaw).
True while a `pointerLock` scene holds the pointer. It turns false when the player presses Escape, which is when a game should pause.
Asks the scene to take the pointer. Call it from the handler of a click, such as a Start or Resume button: a browser allows it only then.
Gives the pointer back, for a menu or a panel opened over the game.
The keys a `<Scene3D gameControls>` holds: `w`, `a`, `s`, `d`, `up`, `down`, `left`, `right`, `space` and `shift`. For other keys, and for touch and a gamepad, use `<Controls>`.

items: Keep what never changes in `staticObjects` and what moves in `objects`. The scenery is then sent to the scene once, not on every tick.
For many copies of one shape, such as a forest or a wall of blocks, use one `"instanced"` object rather than a record for each.
The camera is a record as well. Here it follows the player; the scene turns it with the mouse.

One first-person app at a time. While two apps that use `softn.scene` are open together in SoftN Web, the one opened second is not given the pointer and reads a yaw of 0 until the first is closed: what a scene and its logic say to each other is kept from other apps, and the first to speak has it.

blocks.title: The older window names
blocks.text: These names are the same values that earlier games read and wrote as `window.__scene3dYaw`, `window.__scene3dPitch`, `window.__scene3dLocked`, `window.__scene3dWantLock`, `window.__scene3dReleaseLock` and `window.__softnKeys`. Those still work, and logic that only reads one now sees its value without writing it first. They are shared with the page by logic that runs on the page’s thread, which is every app unless its manifest asks for a worker with `config.execution`; logic in a worker does not see them.

A car, a ball or a character seen from behind needs a camera that keeps up with it. Give the camera a `follow` and the scene places it on every frame it draws, so logic keeps the car and nothing else.

blocks.code:
// Chase: drive round the field with W A S D or the arrows and collect the flags. The camera follows the car. let pad = { presses: {} } let car = { x: 0, z: 0, heading: 0, speed: 0 } let flags = [] let found = 0 let objects = [] // The camera keeps behind the car and looks a little ahead of it. The scene works that out on every frame. let camera = { follow: { target: "car", distance: 7, height: 3.5, lookAhead: 2 }, fov: 60 } // What never changes. items.description: `{ target, distance, height, lookAhead }`: the camera stands `distance` behind the object whose `id` is `target` and `height` above it, and looks `lookAhead` in front of it. Behind is away from the object’s front, which is its +z turned by its `rotation`, so turn the object and the camera comes round.

Between 0 and 1: the share of the way left that the camera covers on each frame. A small value (0.1 to 0.2) lets it trail softly behind, a large one keeps it close, and 0, or leaving it out, puts the camera straight where it should be.

Milliseconds the scene takes to move an object from where the last step left it to where this one put it. With logic stepping thirty times a second (`maxFps={30}`) and a screen drawing sixty or more, `transition={34}` fills the frames between steps, so movement is smooth however fast the screen is. An object can give its own, and `transition: 0` on one makes it jump.
Page content pinned to an object: here the count rides above the car. `clickThrough` lets a click or a drag that starts on it reach the scene.
For an `"instanced"` object: a turn and a size for each copy, as flat lists beside `instances`. Six trees, or six thousand, are one record and one thing drawn.

items: An object can also face a point or lie along a line without any trigonometry: `lookAt: { x, y, z }` turns its front to that point, and `align: { x, y, z }` lays its long axis along that direction (an arrow, a beam, a limb).
`camera: { type: "orthographic", size: 20 }` is a camera with no perspective, for a plan, a board game or a strategy map. `near` and `far` say how close and how far it draws.
With `orbitControls`, `@cameraChange` hands your function where the person left the camera, so the app can show the same view next time.
`@stats` reports frames a second, draw calls and triangles about once a second while you are tuning a scene. Leave it out of the finished game.

blocks.text: A scene of well-made models can still look like a drawing of them. What a photograph has that a plain scene lacks is mostly four things: light arriving from everywhere around the subject and not from one lamp, a little darkness where things touch, a lens that is sharp at one distance, and edges that are not stepped. Each is one prop.

items.description: Light the scene from a picture of its surroundings: a panorama, twice as wide as it is tall, of everything around the place. Its bright parts light the scene from where they are, and it is what metal and glass reflect, which is most of what makes them read as metal and glass. A `.hdr` or `.exr` holds real brightness and gives real light (up to 8192 by 4096); a `.jpg`, `.png` or `.webp` works too. `rotation` (radians) turns it, `blur` (0 to 1) softens what is shown behind the scene, `backgroundIntensity` brightens that, and `environmentIntensity` sets how strongly it lights. Leave `background` out to light the scene with it and keep the scene’s own `background`. With an environment and no `lights`, the environment is the scene’s light; add a directional light with `castShadow` for the sun, since a panorama casts no shadows. `environment="studio"` needs no file: a plain bright room.

The soft darkening where two surfaces meet: a wheel on the ground, a bracket on a panel, the corner of a room. It is what stops a thing looking pasted onto what it stands on. `{ radius: 0.6, intensity: 1 }` sets how far it reaches, in scene units, and how dark it gets. It is the costly effect: about a millisecond a frame on a fast desktop card, and much more on a phone.

A lens: the object whose `id` is `focusOn` is sharp, and what is nearer or farther is blurred, more the farther it is from that distance. The scene measures the distance on every frame, so a camera that moves, or a subject that does, stays in focus. `focus: 4.5` keeps a distance sharp where there is no one object. `aperture` is how fast the blur grows with distance and `maxBlur` where it stops, as a share of the picture: start from these two numbers, and halve both for a subtler lens.

The glow round what is very bright, a darkening toward the corners, and film grain. A little of each; with the light as bright as daylight, raise bloom’s `threshold` until only lamps and glints glow. A scene with effects on keeps its smooth edges.

How the light the scene worked out is turned into the colours a screen can show. `"agx"` and `"aces"` keep bright things from burning out to flat white; the exposure is the lens opening: twice the number is twice as bright.

A directional light draws its shadows inside a box `shadowCameraSize` units each way from where it aims. A small box gives fine shadows and a large one covers more ground, so give a close shot a small one. `follow: "camera"` carries the box with the camera.

items: Move the named parts of a model without a clip: `parts: { Wheel_FL: { rotation: { x: 1.2, y: 0, z: 0 } }, Hatch: { visible: false } }`. Each is measured from the pose the file gives that part, in radians about the part’s own axes. The names are in `nodes` of the model’s "loaded" state (`@modelState`). A playing clip keeps whatever a part is not given.
Particles need not be squares: `particleShape: "round"` draws discs, and `"soft"` discs that fade to nothing at the edge, for dust, smoke, sparks and stars.
Make textures and models at the size they will be seen. A ground seen from knee height wants a texel every millimetre or two; the same texture on a hill a kilometre off wants none of that.
Compare with the real thing. If the scene was made in Blender, render the same frame there and put the two side by side: what differs is what to change.

blocks.text: A scene can be made whole in Blender: its objects and materials, its animation, its cameras with their moves and cuts, its lamps. Exported as one `.glb`, the scene plays it as Blender has it, and the page’s part is the clock.

blocks.code:
// A film made in Blender and exported as one file. This page is its clock. let time = 0 // seconds into the film let length = 0 // how long it is: the file says, once it has loaded let playing = false // What the scene draws: the whole of Blender's scene, held at this second of its animation. // Its own lamps light it and cast its shadows. $: objects = [{ id: "film", type: "model", modelUrl: "assets/film.glb", castShadow: true, receiveShadow: true, animation: { clip: "*", time: time }, lights: { castShadow: true, shadowCameraSize: 20 } }] // The scene says what it loaded. A file from SoftN's export script for Blender carries the // film's record: how long it is, which camera from when, each camera's lens and focus. function loaded(model) { if (model.state === "loaded" && model.film) length = model.film.duration } // One frame of the screen: the film is that much further on. function step(dt) { time = Math.min(length, time + dt) if (time >= length) playing = false } // Play and stop; at the end, from the start again. function toggle() { if (!playing && time >= length) time = 0 playing = !playing } First drive
{time.toFixed(1)} of {length.toFixed(1)} seconds
blocks.caption: A film made in Blender, played from the page’s clock. This is docs/examples/scene-film.ui, which SoftN’s tests play: they tell it the file has loaded, press Play, and check the second each frame hands the scene.

items.description: `time` holds the clip at that many seconds from its first frame, so the app’s own clock runs the film: it can be stopped, stepped a frame at a time and wound to any moment. `clip: "*"` is every clip of the file together, which is what Blender’s default export needs (it writes one clip for each thing that moves); name one clip to play that one alone.

Look through a camera that is in the model whose `id` is `film`: where it stands, which way it faces and how wide its lens is, on every frame, after the clip has moved it. `name: "Cam.Close"` picks one camera. With no name it is the camera the film cuts to at that second (below), or the file’s first. A cut is a cut: nothing is eased across it.

A file’s own lamps shine as the file has them. `lights: { castShadow: true, shadowCameraSize: 20 }` lets its sun and spot lamps cast shadows, in a box kept round what the camera sees; `lights: { intensity: 0.5 }` dims them; `lights: false` switches them off, for a scene that brings its own.

Focus as the camera in force has it in Blender: on the object it was set to follow, or at its distance, with the blur of its f-stop. A camera with no focus set blurs nothing. Without a film’s record, `depthOfField: { focusOn: "rover", fstop: 2.8 }` is a lens in a photographer’s terms: a smaller f-number blurs more.
When the file has loaded, the scene says what is in it: its `clips` and how long each is (`clipLengths`), its `cameras` and `lights` by name, its `nodes`, and the `film` record described next.

blocks.text: Some of what a film is has no place in a `.glb`: which camera the film looks through and from when, a lens that zooms, what a camera is focused on. SoftN’s export script for Blender, `tools/blender/softn_export.py` in SoftN’s repository, exports the scene and writes those into the file as well, where the scene reads them. Blender’s own export works too: the scene then plays through whichever camera the page names.

items: In Blender, bind a timeline marker to a camera wherever the film cuts to it (Marker, Bind Camera to Markers). The script turns the markers into the film’s cuts.

Run it from a terminal: `blender film.blend --background --python softn_export.py -- film.glb`. Beside `film.glb` it writes the world’s panorama (`film.hdr`), for `environment={{ url: "assets/film.hdr" }}`, and `film.softn.json`, the same record for an app that wants it before the model has loaded.
Materials are Blender’s Principled BSDF: colour, metal, roughness, normal, emission, clearcoat and glass all come across. Anything made of procedural nodes is baked to pictures first.

A lamp’s strength comes across as Blender’s number when the export’s lighting mode is Unitless, which the script sets. Blender’s default mode writes numbers 683 times larger, for a renderer with a camera’s exposure: `lights: { intensity: 1 / 683 }` brings such a file back.
Compression: tick Meshopt, not Draco, which this runtime does not read. A file may be up to 32 MB in SoftN Web.
Set the scene’s tone mapping to Blender’s: its default view transform is AgX, which is `toneMapping="agx"`, and an exposure of one stop in Blender is `toneMappingExposure={2}`.

sections.title: When the app goes to the background

blocks.caption: Pause when nobody is looking. From docs/examples/game-dodge.ui.

blocks.text: The runtime calls `_onHide()` when the app is no longer in front of the person: another app was chosen in a host that keeps several open, or the browser’s tab went to the background. It calls `_onShow()` when the app is back. Define either, or neither. An app that starts in the background is told `_onHide()` once, after `_init()`.

items: A `<Loop frame>` and a scene stop by themselves while hidden. `_onHide()` is for what only your game knows: pausing, stopping a sound with `softn.audio.stopAll()`, saving.
Do not resume by yourself in `_onShow()` if the player would be caught out. Show a Resume button, as the example does.
A running game, a paused game in memory and a saved game are three different lifetimes. Decide which of them a reload should bring back, and save that with `localStorage` or XDB.

blocks.text: ZIPP’s browser artifact is interpreter-only; native JIT performance is not a prediction of game performance in a SoftN browser host. Rendering, scene complexity, asset loading, script work and host-boundary traffic can all affect responsiveness.

items: What costs time each tick is the arithmetic in your own logic and the number of separate things drawn, more than the passing of the lists to the page.
A variable the page does not name is not copied to it. Keep bulky working data in variables only logic reads, and hand the page the lists it draws.
If the logic cannot finish in a frame, cap it with `maxFps` rather than letting ticks pile up.
Start with a small scene and one interaction. Measure frame time, startup time and memory on a phone as well as a desktop while adding content.

blocks.title: Rendering and compute are separate
blocks.text: A Three.js scene does not mean the app can use GPU compute. The gpu capability, host support and the host’s grant decide that; Python’s torch runs on the CPU.

sections.title: Check playability, not just a screenshot

items: Make the first action obvious and provide a restart path.
Play with the keyboard, with touch, and with a gamepad if you have one. Check that the page does not scroll under the game.
Switch to another app or tab in the middle of a game and come back.
Keep important text and controls readable on a small viewport.
Test missing audio permission or blocked autoplay where relevant.
Use bundled assets or document the required network resources.
Test the exported bundle for longer than a single successful frame.

blocks.text: For your first game, one reliable loop with a clear outcome is a better test of the platform than a large map with unfinished controls.

pages.title: Machine learning with torch
pages.summary: Train and run small neural networks in a Python app, in the browser, with ZIPP’s torch: declare it, keep tensors in Python and show plain numbers.

seo.title: Machine learning with torch | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Use torch in a SoftN Python app: declare it in manifest.json, train tensors and torch.nn models on the CPU in the browser, show results as state and keep the page responsive.

sections.title: Models that train in the page

blocks.text: A Python app can use ZIPP’s torch: tensors, autograd, `torch.nn` modules, losses and optimizers, running on the CPU inside the engine. Training happens in the visitor’s browser, with no server, account, network access or permission, and the data and model stay on the device.
It suits small models you can train in seconds: fitting a curve, a tiny classifier, a demonstration of gradient descent. It is not a GPU training environment.

blocks.caption: manifest.json: an app that imports torch says so.

blocks.text: Builder offers this as Machine learning (torch) when you create a Python project, and in the Python section of Export. Studio’s brief offers Uses machine learning `torch`. Either preview offers Enable torch if the app imports torch without the declaration.

items: An `import torch` the manifest does not declare is refused with the line to add: “logic/main.py imports torch, which an app asks for in manifest.json: "config": { "python": { "packages": ["torch"] } }”.
A package the runtime does not offer is refused too. torch is the only one.
`torch.py` is a reserved module name: an app file of that name would hide the package.

sections.title: A model in a few lines

blocks.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

xs = torch.tensor([[0.0], [1.0], [2.0], [3.0]])
ys = xs * 2.0 + 1.0
model = nn.Linear(1, 1)
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.05)
loss = 0.0


def train(steps):
    global loss
    for _ in range(steps):
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        current = ((model(xs) - ys) ** 2).mean()
        current.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        loss = float(current)
blocks.caption: logic/main.py: a one-neuron network learns y = 2x + 1.

blocks.code:
<logic src="../logic/main.py" />

<App>
  <Stack direction="vertical" gap="md" padding="lg">
    <Text>Loss: {loss}</Text>
    <Button variant="primary" @click={() => train(50)}>Train 50 steps</Button>
  </Stack>
</App>
blocks.caption: ui/main.ui: each click trains a short batch and shows the loss.

sections.title: Keep tensors in Python, show numbers

blocks.text: Tensors, models and optimizers are Python objects, so they stay in Python and are never mirrored as state. Keep what the markup shows in plain numbers, strings and lists, such as `loss = float(current)` or a rounded weight, and those update the interface like any other state.

The first `import torch` compiles torch’s Python modules: about a second on a desktop, once per page. A training step of a small model takes a few tens of milliseconds and runs on the page’s thread, so train in short calls, from a button or a timer, rather than one long loop that freezes the page.

items: Eager CPU tensors only. `torch.compile`’s GPU path is not connected in SoftN’s Python runtime, so do not use it.
torch here is ZIPP’s own subset of the PyTorch API, not PyTorch itself. The TORCH_COMPATIBILITY.md file in ZIPP’s release bundles lists what it covers.

The first declaring app on a page also downloads the torch package, about 2.2 MB (about 400 KB compressed), once; the runtime adds it before the app compiles, and every later torch app on the page reuses it. Apps that do not declare torch never download it. If the package cannot be loaded, the app is refused by name with the reason, rather than failing at its first import.
Python’s own limits apply: no `async`, main thread only, and state must be JSON data.

blocks.text: `examples/torch-trainer` in the repository trains `nn.Linear` to learn y = 2x + 1 from five points, showing the loss, the learned weight and bias, and a prediction as you train. Build it with `node examples/torch-trainer/build.mjs`, then open `TorchTrainer.softn` in the runtime at `/web/` with the + button, or drop the file on the page.

pages.summary: Understand requested capabilities, host grants, browser consent and the limits of an editable client bundle.

seo.title: Permissions and sandboxing | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Understand SoftN permissions and sandboxing: permission.json, host grants, network allowlists, browser consent and private client-server boundaries.

sections.title: Three questions before an app uses a capability

blocks.text: A useful way to reason about a host operation is to ask: does the app declare it, does this host support and grant it, and does the surrounding browser or service allow it? Those checks can fail independently.
The runtime knows ten capabilities. Each is off until the bundle declares it and the visitor or host grants it, whichever language the app’s logic is written in.

items.description: Network: may call the internet, limited to allowed_hosts; the runtime asks first. This computer and its local network (localhost, 192.168.…, a .local name) are reached only when allowed_hosts names them. A host is named exactly as a URL writes it, in lower case, with no port and no wildcard: `example.com` does not cover `api.example.com`. Only `https` addresses are allowed unless the entry also says `"allow_http": true`, which a machine on the local network reached at an `http://` address needs as well as its name in allowed_hosts.
May take pictures, with the visitor’s permission.
May record audio, with the visitor’s permission.
May read files the visitor chooses and save files it makes.
Scans QR codes with the camera.
Downloads and runs a model in the browser.
Uses the graphics card for compute.

Replicates the app’s database to the visitor’s other devices, by peer sync (`db.startSync`) or through the sync server the manifest names (`config.server.url`). Neither starts without this declaration and the person’s Allow, and when `net` lists allowed_hosts, the sync server’s host must be one of them. `"roomCollections": ["scores"]` limits what every peer-to-peer room of the app carries, both ways, to the collections named, and the consent bar says so; without it a room carries every collection whose name does not start with `_`. A script’s `collections` option may narrow the list, never widen it.
Server storage: keeps records in the app’s own database on the hosting site, shared with everyone running the app unless a collection’s policy says otherwise.

Host acceleration: runs the numeric code it generates on the browser’s own engine, bound to its own data. Only logic that runs in a worker (`config.execution: "worker"`) gets it: on the page’s thread `accel.*` throws as if it were denied. The grant is read as the logic starts; an Allow given after the app opened restarts its logic, which has the grant from then.

blocks.caption: A network permission. api.example.com is a placeholder, not a service SoftN provides.

blocks.text: A declaration requests a capability. It does not authenticate to that API, grant server-side access or prove that a destination is appropriate. Use the smallest set of destinations and operations the app needs.
Treat permission.json as part of the app’s public explanation. Someone opening the bundle should be able to understand why a task planner or media app needs each requested capability.

sections.title: The host boundary is part of the design

blocks.text: Guest logic runs in the ZIPP WebAssembly engine and reaches only the integration points SoftN exposes. ZIPP’s host calls are denied by default, and installing a bridge is not the same as granting authority. Python’s `softn.*` calls go through the same host checks as JavaScript’s.

Sandboxing is an implementation boundary, not a promise that every app or host is risk-free. Host code, app data handling, resource limits and private backend authorisation still need appropriate testing.

blocks.title: No client-side hiding place for secrets
blocks.text: A .softn bundle is editable, inspectable source. Keep service credentials and private server databases in a deployment designed to keep them on the server.

sections.title: What an app is kept from

blocks.text: An app is drawn in the host’s own page, next to the host’s controls and, in the web runtime, other apps. Whatever a bundle declares, it is held to its own part of that page.

items.description: A style block styles the app and nothing else: what each rule styles must be inside the element the app is drawn in, while what is around it may be anything (a theme the host sets still counts), and `html`, `body` and `:root` mean that element. The browser’s own CSS reader checks the result. The app’s `@font-face` and `@keyframes` names are its own. `@import`, `@property`, `@scope` and `@page` are dropped.
Every host draws the app in a box that keeps its paint, so a `position: fixed` element stops at the box and cannot cover the permission bar.

A listener the logic puts on the window hears the keys aimed at the app, or at the page when nothing has focus, and the pointer while the app is on screen: never what is typed into the host or another app.

`alert()` is shown in the app, as the app’s, and not while the permission bar is asking. The browser’s own dialog, which carries the host’s name and holds the whole tab, is never used. A `<dialog>` opened with `showModal()` is drawn over the app inside its box, never in the browser’s top layer.

`softn.net.fetch` sends no cookie and no referring address of the page the app is drawn in, and follows no redirect. An app that signs in sends its own `Authorization` header, or asks the host’s backend. A model or image the AI capability downloads needs `net` as well.

An app may keep 1 MB in `localStorage` and 3 MB of records in the browser’s storage, so one app cannot fill the store the host and every other app share. A write past that is refused, as the browser refuses a full store. Records from a peer-to-peer room may take 2.5 MB of the 3, so the app’s own writes always have room; a record that does not fit stays in the room and on the peers that keep it.

`softn.files.saveFile` saves when the person clicks or presses a key, under a plain file name; a kind of file that runs when it is opened (`.exe`, `.bat`, `.js`, `.lnk` and the like) is saved as text.

blocks.text: A friendly app name is a label, not a storage credential. General bundle loading uses digest-based isolation; configured single-app and FormLogic hosts use their own deployment identity. Test what happens to data and grants when publishing an update.

blocks.text: These pages describe the capability model. They do not certify a deployment’s security or say that any particular host configuration is safe for sensitive records. Review the version, host policy and backend you actually run before deciding that.

seo.title: Offline use, local data and app identity | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Understand offline SoftN apps, browser libraries, local records, bundle seeds, host identity and the limits of local-first persistence.

sections.title: Local-first describes a data approach, not every dependency

blocks.text: SoftN keeps app-scoped XDB records locally and a browser library of the apps you opened, with offline readiness shown for saved apps. That helps a local workflow, but it does not make a remote API or an externally hosted asset available without a connection.
Test the actual app flow offline, not only whether its first screen opens. A form might be local while its submit action or background image still depends on a server.

sections.title: Keep four kinds of state separate

rows: The client source, configuration, seeds and distributable assets
What is currently happening in a live app, such as unfinished input
Data kept by the app’s storage integration and identity
Server-side records governed by that deployment’s access rules
blocks.caption: Exporting or closing one of these does not automatically transfer or preserve the others.

blocks.text: Builder preview data adds another testing context. Use Data view to inspect the seeds you plan to distribute, and check a fresh Runtime instance to see the recipient’s starting experience.

sections.title: Treat the browser library as this browser’s library

blocks.text: The web library keeps the apps opened in this browser. It is not an account-wide library because an app has a name: another profile or host can have a different library and storage.

Keep a separate exported copy of important app source. For important live records, use the backup or export facilities provided by the chosen host and confirm that you can restore them. Do not assume the project export button is a complete record backup.

sections.title: An update can involve identity decisions

blocks.text: The general loader uses bundle digests for isolation. Configured single-app and FormLogic hosts provide their own deployment identity. Before shipping an update, test whether the host treats it as the same app for records and grants.

blocks.title: Test upgrades before replacing a working app
blocks.text: Use a non-production copy with representative records. Check loading, identity, schema changes and the recovery path.

pages.title: Python logic
pages.summary: Write an app’s client logic in Python: link a .py file, keep state in top-level names, change it with global, and call host capabilities through import softn.

seo.title: Python logic | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Write SoftN app logic in Python: .py files, state and global, handlers, modules, import softn, what Python lacks, reserved names and the refusals that explain them.

blocks.text: An app’s client logic can be Python instead of JavaScript. In Builder, choose Python (logic/main.py) as the Logic Language of a new project; in Studio, choose Python in the brief. Or write the file yourself: a logic file whose name ends `.py` is Python, and nothing else says so.

blocks.code:
<logic src="../logic/main.py" />

<App>
  <Stack direction="vertical" gap="md" padding="lg">
    <Input :bind={draft} placeholder="New task" />
    <Button variant="primary" @click={() => add_task()}>Add</Button>
    #each (task in tasks)
      <Text>{task.title}</Text>
    #end
  </Stack>
</App>
blocks.caption: ui/main.ui links its Python module with <logic src>.

blocks.text: Python must be in a file. An inline `<logic lang="python">` block is refused, because Python’s indentation is the program and markup indentation is not reliable. An app uses one language for all its logic.

items.description: A module-level `count = 0` is state the template can read, like a JavaScript `let`. A name starting with `_` is private to the module.
A function that assigns a module-level name must declare it `global`, or Python creates a local and the state never changes. This is the most common surprise when porting from JavaScript.
Every top-level function can be called from the template. `_init()` runs once after the app loads.
`logic/helpers.py` is the module `helpers`; another file reaches it with `import helpers` or `from helpers import double`.

`dict`, `list`, `str`, `int`, `float`, `bool` and `None`. A class instance, tensor or model stays in Python. Integers beyond ±(2⁵³−1) are shown as strings, non-finite floats as `None`, and state is mirrored about thirty levels deep.
A traceback names your own file and line; the runtime’s generated files are left out.

blocks.text: A handler bound by name is passed the event, so `@click={add_task}` calls `add_task(event)`, and a `def` with no parameter for it raises `TypeError`. Bind it through an arrow, `@click={() => add_task()}`, or give the function a parameter. Builder’s handler suggestions insert the arrow form for you.
Inputs write back to state with `:bind={draft}`. `:value={draft}` only shows the value, so typing would never reach your logic.

`import softn` gives Python the capabilities the JavaScript `softn` global offers, under both Python and JavaScript names (`softn.camera.capture_photo` and `softn.camera.capturePhoto`). Capabilities are asynchronous, so each one takes a callback rather than returning its answer.

blocks.code:
import softn

status = ""


def on_saved(response):
    global status
    status = "Saved"


def save(record):
    softn.backend.call("save", record, on_saved)


def on_key(event):
    global status
    status = "Pressed " + event["key"]


softn.on("keydown", on_key)
blocks.caption: A capability hands its answer to a callback; softn.on registers an event listener.

blocks.text: A value passed to `softn.*` must be JSON data. Anything else raises an error rather than being quietly replaced, so a capability call never sends something other than what you wrote.

items: `db.*`, `localStorage` and `navigator.clipboard`: they are JavaScript globals, so Python logic cannot read or write the app’s local records. `softn.storage.*` keeps records on the server, only in an app opened from the directory that publishes it (XDB data, Server storage).
`$:` computed declarations, and any template expression that must be evaluated inside the app’s scope. Call a function instead.
Worker execution. A Python app runs on the page’s main thread.
Server logic. The PHP and Rust hosts run server `.logic` as JavaScript.
`async` and `await`, and the other gaps of ZIPP’s Python subset. It is ZIPP’s own implementation of Python, not CPython, and installs no pip packages; torch is the one package the runtime provides.
