seo.title: Host one app on its own website | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Host a SoftN app on its own website with the single-app runtime: the build and package commands, every runtime.config.json field, permission modes, identity and the archive variants.

sections.title: A website focused on one app

blocks.text: The single-app runtime (apps/softn-single) is a separate entry point that uses the real renderer, component registry, ZIPP sandbox and XDB, and nothing else: no launcher, catalogue, editor, account bar, bundle cache or download controls. Its loader is a spinner, its title comes from configuration, and the shell carries no product branding. Your app’s own interface renders unchanged.
The app remains a SoftN client. Its editable interface and logic are still distinct from any private service it calls, and a custom domain does not change what is delivered to the browser.

blocks.code:
npm ci
npm run build:single
npm run package:single
blocks.caption: Builds the shared packages and the @softn/single workspace, then writes release/softn-app-static-v<version>.zip. Add `-- --with-backend` to also produce the Apache/PHP backend variant.

blocks.text: Upload the contents of the archive to an HTTPS web directory, at the root or in a subdirectory, keeping the adjacent assets paths intact. PHP, the directory API and a service worker are not required. Serve .wasm as application/wasm and .mjs as JavaScript; the included Apache file sets those types and disables directory listing. Other servers need the equivalent MIME settings.
Every release archive starts with a README.md that says what the package is and how to deploy it, and carries the detailed guide beside it.

items.label: Single-app runtime guide
items.description: The repository guide: limits, the preapproved permission mode, the directory-served variant and validation notes.

sections.title: Point the runtime at your app

blocks.text: Replace the sample app.softn in the deployed directory and edit runtime.config.json next to it. The entry always reads its adjacent configuration: query parameters, hashes, file drops and messages cannot replace the chosen app.

blocks.code:
{
  "version": 1,
  "id": "my-application",
  "title": "My application",
  "bundle": "./app.softn",
  "loadingText": "Loading…",
  "theme": "dark"
}
blocks.caption: A minimal runtime.config.json.

items.description: The configuration format; always 1.

The deployment’s stable identity. Local records are keyed by the configuration file’s path plus this value, so keep it the same across updates of the same app and use a different one for a different app.
The document title shown by the browser.
Where the .softn file is, relative to the configuration file. It must be same-origin HTTP(S); redirects, credentials in URLs and fragments are refused.
The text shown with the spinner while the app loads.
The theme for an app whose manifest declares none: `"light"` or `"dark"`, dark when left out. An app whose `config.theme.mode` is light or dark is drawn on that side whatever this says.

Optional path to a same-origin JSON permission declaration, for example ./permission.json. When present it is authoritative; otherwise the runtime uses the bundle’s permission.json, then its legacy manifest declaration, then no permissions. An invalid declaration stops loading.
Optional pin of the exact bundle bytes. Required for the preapproved permission mode.

"prompt" (the default) loads the app with capabilities withheld and shows an unbranded permission bar; "preapproved" enables the declared capabilities immediately for a trusted app and needs a valid sha256 pin.
Only when a directory serves this shell for a published app: the same-origin runs and storage endpoints; the app reaches the second as `softn.storage.*`. A standalone deployment leaves it out.

"app" (the default) pins the app to the viewport and scrolls inside it, for an app that lays out its own screen; "page" lets the document grow and scroll, for an app that reads as a long page. Only the shell changes; the bundle is the same.

Optional path to a same-origin JavaScript module whose default export returns the function the app’s `softn.backend.call(action, input, callback)` reaches. It is for actions that need something only the host should hold, such as a key or a live connection. A named module that fails to load stops the page rather than running without it.

blocks.text: Any other key is refused. Limits: the configuration is capped at 16 KiB, a sidecar permission declaration at 64 KiB and the compressed bundle at 32 MiB; the shared bundle validator also applies its entry and decompression limits, and a startup download fails when nothing arrives for 60 seconds; a slow download that keeps arriving is not cut off.

sections.title: Run a page of your own site, with no bundle

blocks.text: A page of your own site can be the app, as you wrote it: no .softn file and no build. Put the runtime’s folder beside the page (the contents of the archive, here in softn/), and name its loader first in the page’s head. The page is then read by SoftN instead of drawn by the browser: an HTML page with SoftN’s components and syntax in it, whose code is in the files its <script src> tags name and runs in SoftN’s sandbox.

blocks.code:
{notes.length} notes

#each (note in notes) key={note.id}

{note.text}

#end
blocks.caption: index.html, beside softn/, main.js and styles.css. `notes`, `draft` and `add` are main.js’s.

items: The loader fetches the page’s own text and what it names: the code its `<script src>` tags name and what that code imports, the stylesheets its `<link>`s name, the pages it imports, and `xdb/<name>.xdb` for each collection it binds, when the site has one. Pictures are read by the browser from the site, by their paths.

A `manifest.json` and a `permission.json` beside the page are read when the site has them: the manifest for what a page cannot say (an `id`, a theme, Python packages, and in `files.logic` and `files.xdb` the modules and seed files no page names: a Python page’s helper modules are listed there, since `import helpers` names a module, not a file), and the declaration for what the app may use. Without a declaration the app is granted nothing. The loader asks for each of these files, and for `xdb/<name>.xdb` for each collection the page binds; where the site has none, the page loads without it, and some browsers report the request as not found in their console.
Every page of a site shares one store of records, keyed by the site’s folder and the manifest’s `id`.

The loader must be the first script in the head, and a plain one (not async, defer or a module): everything after it is then kept as text, with none of its scripts run and nothing drawn. Placed later, the page is hidden until the app is drawn, but the browser has already run any script written before it, and runs your code files itself as well (where they fail at their first `import` or `export`).
`<script src="softn/softn.js" data-page="app.html"></script>` runs another page of the site in this one’s place.
The runtime’s folder must be on the same site as the page. Scripts and stylesheets from other sites are not loaded.

blocks.text: In prompt mode the app is interactive straight away while a compact bar above it lists the requested access, with expandable details, Allow and Not now. The bar takes its own space rather than covering the app. Dismissing it leaves access disabled and keeps a Review permissions control available without restarting. Allow takes effect in the running app without starting it again: a call that was waiting for the answer is made, and the app’s `_onPermissionChange()`, where it defines one, is called so start-up features can retry. An app that was refused something earlier and defines none is started again with its variables carried over, and the bar says so beforehand.

Consent is scoped to the configuration location, the exact bundle digest and the full permission declaration: changing the app or its host restrictions asks again. Browser camera and microphone prompts stay independent, and the runtime cannot bypass the browser’s own file selection.

blocks.title: Preapproved is a deployment decision
blocks.text: Setting "permissionMode": "preapproved" belongs in runtime.config.json, not in the app manifest. It preserves declared host and file scope restrictions, writes no visitor consent record and requires the sha256 pin, so a swapped bundle is not silently trusted.

The general bundle loader isolates apps by digest; this runtime keys local records by the configuration path plus id, not by the app’s display name. Keep those stable and an updated bundle still sees its records; bundle seeding never overwrites existing records.

Test an update with disposable records before changing a live deployment. Confirm the new version opens the same data and check how schema or seed changes affect an existing user. Manifest-defined server synchronisation is not enabled automatically by this host.

sections.title: Three ways to ship one app

items: Static: `softn-app-static-v<version>.zip`. HTML, the engine and your bundle, on any HTTPS host.

Static with a private backend: `softn-app-static-with-backend-linux-x64-v<version>.zip` adds a `backend/` folder with softn-runner, which answers each request without Node, a bundled Linux x64 Node for operator request hooks and the WebSocket bridge, SQLite and the ZIPP engine, behind Apache and PHP and enabled by the operator. The release archive carries softn-runner; one you build with `npm run package:single -- --with-backend` carries it only when given `--runner-dir apps/softn-runner/dist` (where `node apps/softn-runner/build.mjs --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` writes the runner and its licences), and without it every request runs on the bundled Node.

Served privately: `softn-app-private-v<version>.zip` keeps the `.softn` in a private directory and serves the page and each entry from PHP, so the archive is never on a URL. `softn-app-private-with-backend-linux-x64-v<version>.zip` is that variant with the backend.

For access-controlled delivery, put the whole deployment behind server-side authentication.

seo.title: Private backends and server-side logic | SoftN Docs
seo.description: SoftN private backends: server-side JavaScript .logic and SQLite on the Rust and PHP hosts, kept apart from client bundles, private scripts, credentials and databases.

sections.title: When an app needs a server

blocks.text: A local app does not need a backend. A server becomes useful when records are shared under authentication, when a private service credential is needed, or when an operation must be controlled outside the editable client.

The repository has two server hosts that run server-side `.logic` with SQLite: the Rust private backend (`apps/softn-host-rust`) and the PHP host (`apps/softn-host-php`), which the single-app backend archives package. Server logic is JavaScript on both; Python is client logic only. FormLogic is a separate connected host with its own configuration.

rows: Authorises requests and enforces access rules
Collects and validates input for usability
Validates input before using private resources
Owns private credentials and server database access
Defines the operation’s durable result and errors
blocks.caption: A responsibility split for a connected app. A client export does not provision a server.

blocks.text: A server resource packaged for deployment is not a script the browser runs. The client should know which operation to request, not carry a private database or service secret.

sections.title: Private serving is not secret client code

blocks.text: The PHP-served single-app archive keeps the original bundle outside the public directory. That is useful deployment hygiene, but anything sent to a browser remains inspectable.

blocks.title: Review the public output
blocks.text: Before deploying, inspect both the downloadable client bundle and the public web directory. Keep private server scripts, credentials and databases out of client downloads.

Start with a few named operations whose inputs, outputs and authorisation rules are easy to state. A planner might need a create-task operation and a list-visible-tasks operation, with the server deciding what the signed-in person can see.

On the Rust and PHP hosts, client logic reaches such an operation through one of the manifest’s `/api/` routes, with `softn.net.fetch` and the site’s own absolute URL (`https://your.site/api/tasks`), so its `permission.json` needs `net` and, when it lists allowed_hosts, the site’s host. `softn.backend.call(action, input, callback)`, in JavaScript or Python, reaches a backend that the page supplies to the app itself: a single-app host module or FormLogic, where the action names are yours. Anywhere else, the Rust and PHP hosts included, it answers `{ error: "This app has no connected backend." }`.

items: Check unauthenticated and unauthorised requests through the host’s test path.
Validate malformed and incomplete input on the server.
Make timeout and unavailable-service messages understandable.
Decide what happens when someone submits twice or retries an uncertain result.
Test database recovery and an app-version upgrade before relying on important data.

blocks.text: This guide is an introduction, not a certification of a deployment’s security. Review the host, version and backend you actually run before handling sensitive information.

pages.title: SoftN and FormLogic
pages.summary: Understand the difference between exporting an editable starter and running an authenticated connected workspace.

seo.title: SoftN and FormLogic | SoftN Docs
seo.description: SoftN and FormLogic: editable starter exports with local XDB, connected iframe apps, softn.backend.call and named backend actions owned by the host, and engine choice.

blocks.text: SoftN supplies the editable app and runtime. FormLogic is a hosted workspace for forms, records, backend actions and app databases. Connecting them does not remove the client-server boundary.

There are two integration paths: converting a supported form into a local-first starter app, and running an app as a connected workspace under FormLogic. Choose the path before assuming what an export contains.
The FormLogic adapter converts supported form schemas into editable `.softn` bundles. The starter keeps its data in local XDB with sync off, and leaves out responses, credentials and access grants.
A starter is an app structure, not a copy of a live account or a connection to the original form’s private data. Inspect it, customise it and test its local record workflow.

blocks.title: An export is not an access grant
blocks.text: Downloading the client does not transfer permission to a live FormLogic backend.

The connected host renders app source in an isolated iframe. Client logic calls named backend actions with `softn.backend.call(action, input, callback)`, while the parent host owns authentication and applies the app’s permissions.

Action names and input shapes belong to the workspace, so check them in its source for the version you deploy. A workspace owner can also choose ZIPP’s smaller JavaScript-only engine; a Python app is refused there by name.

`examples/formlogic-workspace` and `examples/aokie-workspace` are editable workspace apps. Aokie’s brings calls, appointments, messages, follow-ups and transcripts into one interface, while the communication services stay part of the host integration.
A workspace example shows a client experience. Downloading the bundle does not provision telephony, authenticated records or the external services it displays.

sections.title: Keep server resources on the hosting platform

blocks.text: For custom server logic and SQLite, configure those resources on the hosting platform and expose the operations the client needs. Keep private scripts, credentials and databases on the server.

FormLogic fetches verified ZIPP engine bytes once per page and gives each isolated execution context its own copy, instance, memory and permissions. Shared engine delivery is not a shared app-data context.

blocks.text: The directory checks a bundle at publication: the manifest needs a `name`, a `version` and a `main` entry that exists, the files it lists must be present, and an unknown `config.python.packages` entry is refused. To exercise publishing locally, the development launcher needs PHP on your PATH.

An app in the directory takes `git push`. Publish its first version on the Publish page, which shows its edit key and these commands with the app’s name in them. If your project is already in git, `git archive --format=zip -o app.softn HEAD` makes that first bundle. The folder’s top level is the bundle’s: `manifest.json` is there. That bundle holds every committed file, `.gitignore` and `.github/` among them, which a push leaves out: `git archive --format=zip -o app.softn HEAD -- . ":(exclude,glob)**/.git*" ":(exclude,glob)**/.git*/**"` leaves out git’s own files and folders, in every folder. The Publish page refuses a file that looks like it holds secrets, as a push does.

blocks.code:
git remote add softn https://my-app@softn.com/api/git/my-app.git
git config --unset remote.softn.fetch
git config remote.softn.push HEAD:refs/heads/main
git config remote.softn.skipFetchAll true
git config http.postBuffer 64M
git push softn
blocks.caption: Run the first five once in a project. From then on, `git push softn` publishes the commit you are on, from any branch. When git asks for a password, give it the app’s edit key. These lines run as they are in Command Prompt, PowerShell and Git Bash.

items: Each push to `main` is a new version, made of the files in that commit, with the commit’s subject as its notes. The same checks as the Publish page apply, and a refusal says why in the terminal. Pushing the files the latest version already has makes no new version, whether that version was pushed or came from the Publish page.

Each app has its own key, generated by the directory. The app’s name in the address is what lets git keep each app’s key apart, where it keeps passwords. Leave the key itself out of the address: it would sit in plain text in the repository’s config.

Everything in the commit you push is public. A file that looks like it holds secrets, such as `.env`, a `.pem` or a `.key`, is refused. So is a backup of edit keys, under any name, and any file that holds the edit key of an app in the directory, this app’s or another’s: save the backup file, and any note of your keys, somewhere outside the project. The refusal names the file. If such a file was ever published, replace the key on the app’s update page. Links and submodules are refused too, as a published app holds its own files.
Git’s own files are left out of the version, in every folder: `.gitignore`, `.gitattributes`, `.gitkeep`, `.github/` and anything else whose name begins with `.git`.

Earlier commits are not kept: the directory keeps the version and nothing of the history. For the same reason `git clone` and `git pull` are not offered. Download an app’s source from its page. In a project whose only remote is the directory, `git pull` has nowhere else to ask, and there is nothing to pull.

Because it keeps no history, the directory cannot refuse a push that is not built on the version that is live, as a git server would. It publishes the push, and says so in the terminal when the live version’s commit is not in the history you pushed: changes someone else published, or you published from another computer, are then not in the new version. Bring them into your project and push again. A push that carries no history, such as a shallow clone’s, is not told this, and neither is a push after a version that came from the Publish page.
Tags are not kept. A push that sends tags along, as git does with `push.followTags`, publishes `main` all the same and says that the tags were not kept.

If the app is one folder of a larger repository, publish that folder alone: `git push softn "HEAD:app:refs/heads/main"`, with the folder’s path in place of `app`. Its first bundle is `git archive --format=zip -o app.softn HEAD:app`. A push of the whole repository says which folder has a `manifest.json`.

To publish from CI, such as a GitHub Actions workflow, keep the key as a secret in an environment variable, here `SOFTN_EDIT_KEY`, and have git read it from there. This one is written for the POSIX shell that CI runs: `git -c credential.helper='!f() { echo "password=$SOFTN_EDIT_KEY"; }; f' -c http.postBuffer=64M push https://my-app@softn.com/api/git/my-app.git HEAD:refs/heads/main`. The key is then in no command line, address or config file. The shallow checkout CI makes is enough, and so is one of a single commit with no branch, which CI often makes.

A push sends the whole history, and one past 50,000 objects or 256 MB is refused. To send only the latest files, without changing your branch: `git push softn "HEAD^{tree}:refs/heads/main"`. That pushes the files of the commit you are on with none of its history, so the version has no notes. It and the command for a folder run as they are in Command Prompt, PowerShell and Git Bash.
An app keeps its first version and its latest ones, 50 in all. Past that, each new version takes the place of the oldest after the first, and the push says which went.

This is for the `git` command, which is what most editors and desktop tools run. Tools built on another git library may not be able to publish a push of any size on some servers, and they are told so. The update page always works.

Files kept in Git LFS are not taken: git sends a pointer to each one, not the file, and a push that holds one is refused. Take the app’s files out of LFS with `git lfs migrate export --include="*.png" --everything`, naming the files you track, and push again. That rewrites the commits that hold them, so a copy of the project elsewhere needs a forced push after it. Or publish from the update page.
If a key may have been seen, replace it on the app’s update page. The next push asks for the new one.

A project set up before `git config --unset remote.softn.fetch` was one of the lines above needs it run once. Without it, git itself refuses `git push --force-with-lease softn` as stale after the first push.

blocks.text: Open the resulting app page and player as a fresh visitor. Confirm the title, description, screenshot and requirements match the running release. Test the public path rather than assuming that a successful local preview confirms publishing.
For a custom website, follow the single-app route. For authenticated private operations, treat backend deployment and permission checks as separate release steps.

pages.title: Publish with your AI agent
pages.summary: Have an AI agent build an app and prepare it for the directory, through a FormLogic site’s MCP server, with you approving before anything is public.

seo.title: Publish with your AI agent | SoftN Docs
seo.description: An AI agent builds a SoftN app on a FormLogic site, prepares a draft for the directory and hands you an approval link. What is public, what is not.

sections.title: Two ways an AI can help

blocks.text: Studio writes and changes an app with the AI you connect, in your browser; publishing it is your step, on the Publish page. An AI agent can also work through a FormLogic site’s MCP server: it builds the app there as a hosted SoftN app, prepares a draft for a SoftN directory, and gives you a link. Nothing is public until you approve it on that link.

items.title: Connect your agent to a FormLogic site
items.text: Add the site’s MCP server to your AI client and sign in with your FormLogic account (OAuth). The site’s administrator must have named a SoftN directory for it to publish to, and set a data encryption key on the server, which keeps the directory’s edit keys.

items.title: Ask for the app
items.text: The agent reads softn_get_started, builds the app as a hosted SoftN app on the site, and checks it there.

items.title: The agent prepares a draft
items.text: softn_create_draft packs the app’s files as a .softn bundle and checks it: its size, file names, manifest and the permissions it declares. Its backend files stay on FormLogic. Nothing is public yet.

items.title: You approve
items.text: softn_publish_draft gives the agent an approval link for you. The page shows where the app goes, who can see it, its listing, what it may use, the files that go public and the bundle’s hash, and links to the app so you can try it. Only you, signed in, can publish it from there. A draft is the files as they were when it was made: if the app changes afterwards, the agent makes a new draft.

items.title: It is listed
items.text: The agent reads back the app’s page and play links. Later versions go the same way: the agent prepares one, and you approve it.

sections.title: What becomes public, and what does not

items: Public: everything in the bundle (its pages, logic, styles and assets, readable by anyone) and its listing (name, description, category, tags).

Not in the bundle: what FormLogic never serves to a browser (the app’s server/, backend/ and private/ folders, .sql files and the manifest’s server settings) and its records. The directory’s copy runs in the browser alone, and the draft says so when the app has a backend.
Kept private: the edit key the directory gives when the app is published. The FormLogic site keeps it encrypted for your account, to publish your later versions, and never shows it to the agent.
Never put API keys, passwords or private data in an app’s files: a bundle is source anyone can read.

blocks.text: Any client that can connect to a remote MCP server over HTTPS, sign in with OAuth 2.1, and call tools that make changes. Whether a particular product and plan lets an agent use tools that make changes is that product’s to say: check its current documentation before relying on it.

blocks.code:
Build me a simple appointment booking app as a hosted SoftN app on this FormLogic site.
Check it works, then prepare it for the SoftN directory as "Booking", category "productivity",
with a one-sentence description. Do not put any keys, passwords or private data in its files.
Give me the approval link, and tell me its page and play links once I have approved it.
blocks.caption: Change the app, the name and the category to yours. The agent can only ask; you publish.

blocks.title: Without an agent
blocks.text: Publish a .softn yourself on the Publish page, or with one request to the directory’s API, as Publishing describes.

seo.title: Develop SoftN from source | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Develop SoftN from source: Node.js 24.19 or newer, npm workspaces, the root scripts, the ZIPP v0.0.35 engine installed by fetch:zipp, tests, and editing these guides.

blocks.text: The root package declares npm workspaces for `packages/@softn/*`, `apps/*` and `e2e`, and requires Node.js 24.19 or newer (`"node": ">=24.19.0"`).

blocks.code:
git clone https://github.com/f2i-com/softn.com.git
cd softn.com
npm ci
npm run build:packages
npm run dev
blocks.caption: Install, build the shared packages and start the development launcher.

blocks.text: The launcher serves everything from one origin, normally http://localhost:1420: the site and these guides itself, and `/web/`, `/builder/`, `/studio/` and `/demos/` through its proxy. It moves to the next free port when one is taken, and starts the PHP directory API at `/api/` only when `php -v` succeeds.

Install the ZIPP engine release; add `-- --check` to re-verify it offline
Fetch demos and the engine if missing, then run the Node and workspace tests
Build the whole site, guides included

blocks.text: A successful docs build is not evidence that the apps build or their tests pass. Run the relevant commands when you change application code.

sections.title: The browser engine comes from a ZIPP release

blocks.text: The engine is not committed. `packages/@softn/core/wasm-zipp` is installed from the ZIPP release that the `zipp-vm` tag in `apps/softn-host-rust/Cargo.toml` names, today v0.0.35, and verified against that release’s SHA256SUMS, so a browser build needs no Rust toolchain. The build, test, typecheck and licence scripts install it when it is missing, and `SOURCE.json` records its provenance and checksums. Offline, point `ZIPP_RELEASE_DIR` at a folder holding the release files.

`packages/@softn/core/src/runtime/vm-adapter.ts` is where the engine is selected. The separate `build:zipp-wasm` workspace script builds an unreleased engine for local experiments only; no release accepts it, and it needs the matching Rust, wasm-bindgen and optimisation tooling.

blocks.code: npm run test -w @softn/core -- test/zipp-languages.test.ts test/zipp-lifecycle.test.ts
blocks.caption: The checks that run JavaScript and Python against the real engine.

sections.title: Choose tests around what you changed

blocks.text: For a UI change, exercise rendering, state updates and export and reopen. For a data change, test empty seeds, existing records and identity across updates. For a host bridge, test unsupported and denied capabilities as well as the successful path. For Python, test the composer’s refusals as well as a working app.
Some commands fetch demos or need local browsers and services; read their definitions in `package.json` before adding one to CI.
Every guide is authored in `docs/content/softn-docs.json` and generated into static pages; there is no second copy of the text. While `npm run dev` runs, `/docs/` rebuilds within a second of an edit.

blocks.code:
npm run docs:validate   # schema and cross-reference checks
npm run docs:test       # the generator's own tests
npm run docs:build      # write the pages and refresh the homepage cards
npm run docs:preview    # build, then serve http://127.0.0.1:4173/docs/
blocks.caption: The documentation scripts.

blocks.text: When a feature changes, update its guide, the page’s `updatedAt` and its source references, and keep version-specific facts, such as the engine release, tied to the artifact that ships.

pages.title: Troubleshooting SoftN apps
pages.summary: Identify whether a problem belongs to the interface, logic, data, permissions, assets or host before changing several layers.

seo.title: Troubleshooting SoftN apps | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Troubleshoot SoftN apps: loading, state updates, Python refusals and handlers, records, permissions, audio, offline use, responsive layouts and backend connections.

sections.title: Find the layer before changing the app

blocks.text: A blank screen, missing record or failed request can come from different layers. First work out whether the problem is in the exported bundle, the UI source, the logic, local records, permission state, asset delivery or host configuration.
Reproduce it with the smallest app or interaction you can. Keep the original export so you can compare a failing change with a working copy.

items.title: Read the refusal
items.text: An app that breaks a composition rule, such as mixing languages or importing torch undeclared, is refused with a message naming the file. Builder and Studio show the same message in their previews.

items.title: Check the artifact
items.text: Open the exact exported .softn file you plan to share, not only the editor project.

items.title: Check the host
items.text: Confirm the target supports the bundle and its required capabilities.

items.title: Check delivery
items.text: For a website, confirm the intended bundle, assets and matching engine files are served.

rows: The handler was bound by name and passed the event. Use `@click={() => fn()}` or give the function a parameter.
Add `global name` to the function that assigns it.
Typing does not reach the logic
Bind the input with `:bind={x}`; `:value` only shows the value.
“… imports torch, which an app asks for in manifest.json”
Declare torch in `config.python.packages`, or use Enable torch in the preview.
Rename the file: `softn`, `torch`, `json`, `math` and `__softn` names are taken.
“This app mixes Python and JavaScript logic”
Move all the logic into one language.
Move the code into a `.py` file and link it with `<logic src>`.
Those are JavaScript globals. From Python, `softn.storage.*` keeps records on the server, and only in an app opened from the directory that publishes it.
blocks.caption: The composer’s messages name the file they are about.

sections.title: The button works but the screen does not change

blocks.text: Check that the template binds the intended function, that the function changes the intended state and that the displayed expression reads that state. Reduce the action to one simple state change before adding database or network work.

A handler receives plain data, never the live DOM event: `event.target.value` is the value the field held, and `event.preventDefault()` does nothing in logic. Cancel a default with a modifier, `@submit.prevent`, and keep what a field holds in bound state.

sections.title: The records look missing or different

blocks.text: Tell apart Builder preview test records, exported seeds and live Runtime records. Then check the host identity: a bundle digest, a single-app identity and a FormLogic deployment are not the same storage context.
Do not clear storage as a first step when it holds important records. Keep a recoverable copy through the host’s own facilities before testing destructive changes.

Check the declaration, host support, the host’s grant and any browser or service consent separately. A network allowlist does not authenticate to a server, and a browser microphone approval does not prove the app declared the capability.

sections.title: Sound does not play on first load

blocks.text: Browsers block sound until the person interacts. A one-shot reports that it was blocked, and a looped track waits for the first click or keystroke. Offer a clear Start action and check that the bundled path exists.

sections.title: It works in preview but not elsewhere

blocks.text: For layout differences, test the exact viewport and theme rather than assuming the preview rewrites the app. For offline differences, check remote assets and backend calls as well as the host’s offline readiness.
For a connected app, confirm the backend and authentication context exist on the target host. A client export does not carry a live backend session.

items: What you expected and what happened instead.
The smallest steps that reproduce it.
The app version, host, browser and operating system.
Whether it fails in preview, in the exported bundle, or both, and the exact refusal message if there is one.
A minimal sanitised bundle or source excerpt, when it is appropriate to share.

blocks.text: Keep credentials, private records and personal capture data out of public issue reports.

pages.title: SoftN frequently asked questions
pages.summary: Straight answers about the app format, accounts, AI, local data, hosting, JavaScript and Python.

seo.title: SoftN frequently asked questions | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Answers to common SoftN questions: .softn files, AI providers, Builder, Runtime, local data, hosting, FormLogic, JavaScript and Python logic, and torch.

blocks.text: An open-source UI language, visual builder and runtime for editable web and desktop apps. A `.softn` bundle brings the interface, logic, data seeds and assets together so the app can be reopened and customised.

A ZIP-based portable app bundle. It usually holds `manifest.json`, `permission.json`, UI source, logic in JavaScript or Python, optional XDB seeds and assets. The manifest needs only a name and a main entry; Builder and Studio write the rest for you.

sections.title: Do I need an AI account?

blocks.text: No. You can try Fieldnotes, build in Builder, open Studio’s examples or write source by hand without one. Studio’s generation uses a provider you choose: Anthropic, any OpenAI-compatible service or a local model. A hosted provider can have its own credentials, limits and charges.

sections.title: Do I have to write code?

blocks.text: Builder offers visual design, data modelling and preview, and Studio can generate a starting point. Source stays available for behaviour that needs direct editing. It is fairer to promise an editable visual-and-code workflow than an app that never needs code.

XDB keeps app-scoped local records through the host, which decides persistence, native storage and sync. A connected backend can keep separate server-owned records. Bundle seeds and someone’s live records are not the same thing.

The browser library shows offline readiness for saved apps. A particular app may still depend on remote assets or backend operations, so test its real workflow without a connection before relying on it.
It is JavaScript, but it runs inside the ZIPP engine with the APIs the host exposes. There is no unrestricted DOM access, no Node.js API and no automatic support for npm packages.

sections.title: Can I write logic in Python?

blocks.text: Yes. Link a `.py` file with `<logic src>`, or choose Python in Builder’s new-project dialog or Studio’s brief. Top-level names are state, functions assign them with `global`, and `import softn` reaches host capabilities. An app uses one language, and server logic stays JavaScript.

sections.title: Can an app do machine learning?

blocks.text: Yes, on a small scale. A Python app can declare torch in its manifest and train models on the CPU in the browser, with tensors, autograd, `torch.nn` and optimizers. It is ZIPP’s torch subset, not a GPU environment.

sections.title: Can I put an app on its own domain?

blocks.text: Yes, with the single-app runtime. Configure its `runtime.config.json`, keep the deployment identity stable, and keep any private backend resources apart from the public client.
No. It is an optional connected host. FormLogic can export local-first starter apps, and it can run authenticated workspaces that call named backend actions.

sections.title: Can I hide an API key in the bundle?

blocks.text: No. Treat every client bundle as inspectable. Keep service credentials on a server and expose only the authorised operations the client needs. A custom domain or a private source archive does not make material sent to a browser secret.
Yes, under the Apache-2.0 licence. When redistributing a complete app or deployment, also review its assets, dependencies and notices, which may have their own terms.

sections.title: Are these docs a complete API specification?

blocks.text: No. They cover workflows and concepts, checked against the repository source, with links to the underlying files. They are not an exhaustive property reference; check the exact version you deploy for host configuration details.
